# installation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/getting-started/installation.mdx

title: "Installation"
description: "Get NeoHaskell running in under five minutes. Install Determinate Nix, clone the template, run nix develop."
sidebar:
  order: 1

import { Steps, Tabs, TabItem, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You are five minutes away from a working NeoHaskell environment. The whole installation is three steps:

1. Install [Determinate Nix](https://determinate.systems/nix).
2. Add yourself to Nix's trusted users list.
3. Clone the NeoHaskell template and run `nix develop` inside it.

That's the whole thing. No compiler toolchain to install by hand. No version juggling. Nix takes care of the compiler, the standard library, the editor integration, and the build tooling. You do not need to know anything about Nix to use it — treat it as a black box that gives you a working shell.

## What you'll have at the end

- A shell where `cabal build`, `cabal run`, `cabal test`, and your editor's language server all work.
- The NeoHaskell template project on your disk, ready to modify.
- A fully-specified environment pinned to a known-good set of tool versions.

## What you don't need

<Aside type="note" title="Things people assume they need — and don't">
- **Docker or Kubernetes.** Not now, not for deployment, not ever unless you want to.
- **A compiler installed separately.** Nix provides it.
- **Any build tool configured by hand.** Nix provides those too.
- **Prior Nix experience.** You will run exactly three Nix commands in this guide and none afterwards.
- **An existing project to adapt.** The template is self-contained.
</Aside>

## Supported platforms

NeoHaskell runs on:

- **macOS** (Apple Silicon and Intel)
- **Linux** (x86_64 and ARM64)
- **Windows via WSL2** (install Determinate Nix inside WSL, not on Windows directly)

If you are on Windows without WSL, [follow Microsoft's WSL2 setup guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) first, then come back.

## Step 1 — Install Determinate Nix

Determinate Nix is a polished installer for Nix with sensible defaults. It is the fastest way to get a working Nix installation.

<Tabs syncKey="platform">
  <TabItem label="macOS / Linux / WSL">
    Run this command in your terminal:

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://install.determinate.systems/nix | sh -s -- install
    ```

    The installer will ask you a few questions. Accept the defaults unless you know you want something different. When it finishes, close your terminal and open a new one — this refreshes your `PATH` so the `nix` command is available.

    Verify the installation:

    ```bash
    nix --version
    ```

    You should see a line like `nix (Determinate Nix 3.x.x)`.
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

<Aside type="tip" title="Already have Nix?">
If you already have Nix installed from another source (nix.org, Lix, etc.), you do not need to reinstall. Just make sure **flakes are enabled** in your `nix.conf`:

```conf
experimental-features = nix-command flakes
```

Determinate Nix has flakes on by default, which is why we recommend it.
</Aside>

## Step 2 — Add yourself as a trusted user

Nix runs build workers in a sandbox. To let the NeoHaskell template use its shared binary cache (which makes the first `nix develop` take about two minutes instead of thirty), you need to be on the trusted users list.

<Steps>
1. **Edit the Nix daemon config file.** Its location depends on your install:

   ```bash
   sudo nano /etc/nix/nix.conf
   ```

2. **Add a line** with your username (replace `your-username` with the output of `whoami`):

   ```conf
   trusted-users = root your-username
   ```

   If the line already exists, append your username after the existing ones, separated by a space.

3. **Restart the Nix daemon.** On macOS:

   ```bash
   sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/org.nixos.nix-daemon
   ```

   On Linux with systemd:

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl restart nix-daemon
   ```
</Steps>

You only need to do this once per machine.

## Step 3 — Clone the template and enter the dev shell

<Steps>
1. **Clone the NeoHaskell starter template** to a directory of your choice:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/neohaskell/template my-first-app
   cd my-first-app
   ```

2. **Enter the development shell:**

   ```bash
   nix develop
   ```

   The first time you run this, Nix downloads GHC, the NeoHaskell core library, and all build tooling. This takes a couple of minutes on a decent internet connection. The output will look busy — a lot of files scroll by, and Nix asks to use the binary cache (say yes).

   When it finishes, your shell prompt will change to indicate you are inside the dev shell. You now have `cabal`, `ghc`, `hlint`, `fourmolu`, and every other tool the project uses.

3. **Verify everything works:**

   ```bash
   cabal build
   ```

   The first build compiles the example application. On modern hardware this takes about thirty seconds. Subsequent builds are incremental and much faster.

4. **Run the example:**

   ```bash
   cabal run
   ```

   You should see the example app start up. If it does, you're done — your environment is ready.
</Steps>

## What the template gives you

The template is a minimal, runnable application structured the way you'll structure real projects:

```text
my-first-app/
├── flake.nix              # Nix environment (don't modify unless you know why)
├── cabal.project          # Cabal build config
├── my-app.cabal           # Package definition
├── src/
│   ├── App.hs             # Application entry point
│   └── MyApp/
│       ├── Config.hs      # Typed configuration
│       └── Domain/        # Your commands, events, entities, queries
├── tests/
│   └── Spec.hs            # Test entry point
└── uploads/               # File upload directory (if using file uploads)
```

You will spend nearly all your time in `src/MyApp/Domain/`. The other files you'll modify once during setup and then rarely touch.

## Editor setup

NeoHaskell works with any editor that supports its language server (HLS, which the template ships with).

<Tabs syncKey="editor">
  <TabItem label="VS Code">
    Install the language server extension for NeoHaskell from the VS Code marketplace (search for "HLS"). When you open the project inside the `nix develop` shell, the extension will pick up the language server automatically.

    To make VS Code always use the dev shell, install [`direnv`](https://direnv.net/) and the VS Code **direnv** extension, then run:

    ```bash
    echo "use flake" > .envrc
    direnv allow
    ```

    Now opening the project folder in VS Code automatically loads the dev shell — no `nix develop` needed.
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Neovim">
    Any LSP-capable config works. The easiest path is [nvim-lspconfig](https://github.com/neovim/nvim-lspconfig) configured to use HLS as the LSP server. Run Neovim from inside the `nix develop` shell so it finds the server on your `PATH`.

    Or, as with VS Code, use [`direnv`](https://direnv.net/) and launch Neovim from the project directory — direnv loads the shell transparently.
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Emacs">
    Use [`lsp-mode`](https://emacs-lsp.github.io/lsp-mode/) or [`eglot`](https://github.com/joaotavora/eglot) pointed at HLS. Launch Emacs from the dev shell, or use [`envrc-mode`](https://github.com/purcell/envrc) to load the shell automatically on project visits.
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Other">
    Any editor with LSP support works. Configure it to run HLS as the LSP server for `.hs` files, and make sure the editor launches from inside the `nix develop` shell (or uses direnv).
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Daily workflow

Once installed, your daily loop looks like this:

```bash
cd my-first-app
nix develop           # Enter the dev shell (skipped automatically if you use direnv)
cabal build           # Build
cabal test            # Run tests
cabal run             # Run the example
```

If you forget `nix develop` and run `cabal build` outside the shell, it will fail because `cabal` is not on your `PATH` — that's expected. The dev shell is what makes everything work.

## Troubleshooting

### "command not found: nix" after installation

Close your terminal and open a new one. The installer adds Nix to your shell's init scripts, which only take effect on new sessions.

### "experimental features 'nix-command flakes' are disabled"

You installed Nix from a source other than Determinate, and flakes are off by default. Edit `~/.config/nix/nix.conf` (creating it if needed) and add:

```conf
experimental-features = nix-command flakes
```

### `nix develop` takes forever

The first run downloads a few hundred megabytes of toolchain. If it feels stuck but your network traffic is still flowing, it is working — just slow. If you haven't completed Step 2 (trusted users), you'll miss the binary cache and have to build GHC from source, which takes much longer. Double-check the trusted-users line before retrying.

### Editor does not find the language server

Your editor is not launching from inside the `nix develop` shell. Either launch your editor from a terminal that already ran `nix develop`, or set up `direnv` as described in the editor section.

### Windows without WSL

NeoHaskell does not support native Windows directly. Install WSL2, run Ubuntu or Debian inside it, and follow the Linux instructions.

### Still stuck?

- Check the [NeoHaskell Discord](https://discord.gg/wDj3UYzec8) — active channel, fast responses.
- [Open an issue](https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/issues).

## Next steps

You have a working NeoHaskell environment. Now choose your path:

- [**Your first events**](/getting-started/first-events/) — ten-minute walkthrough that records an event, reads it back, and derives state from it.
- [**Build NeoBank**](/tutorial/) — a full tutorial that builds a banking service from scratch.
- [**Reading NeoHaskell**](/getting-started/reading-neohaskell/) — if you want to get comfortable with the syntax before touching code.

# reading-neohaskell.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/getting-started/reading-neohaskell.mdx

title: "Reading NeoHaskell"
description: "A visual tour of NeoHaskell syntax for developers coming from mainstream languages. Read any NeoHaskell file without prior functional-programming background."
sidebar:
  order: 3

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You opened a NeoHaskell file for the first time and the syntax felt alien. That's normal. In five minutes, it won't.

Strongly-typed functional languages have a reputation for unreadable symbols. NeoHaskell deliberately sheds most of that. What's left is a small, consistent set of building blocks. Here they are, with what each one means in languages you probably already know.

## The dictionary

| You see | In NeoHaskell this means | In JS/TS, think… |
|---|---|---|
| `data Foo = Foo { a :: Int, b :: Text }` | Define a record type with two fields | `type Foo = { a: number, b: string }` |
| `data Result = Ok | Err` | Define a sum type (either Ok or Err) | `type Result = { kind: "ok" } \| { kind: "err" }` |
| `case value of` | Pattern match — exhaustive switch | `switch (value.kind)` — but enforced |
| `let x = 5` | Bind a local value | `const x = 5` |
| `x |> f |> g` | Apply `f` to `x`, then `g` to the result | `g(f(x))` (or `x.then(f).then(g)` conceptually) |
| `func arg1 arg2` | Call `func(arg1, arg2)` | `func(arg1, arg2)` |
| `do { ... }` | Sequence of steps inside a `Task` | `async () => { ... }` |
| `Task.yield x` | Return `x` from an async-style block | `return x` |
| `Task.throw e` | Fail with error `e` | `throw e` |
| `-- comment` | Line comment | `// comment` |
| `{- ... -}` | Block comment | `/* ... */` |

If you memorize that table, you can read any NeoHaskell file. Seriously — that's almost the whole syntax.

## An annotated tour

Here is a real command file. We'll walk through it line by line.

```haskell
module MyApp.Cart.Commands.AddItem (
  AddItem (..),
  decide,
) where
```

**What you see:** A module declaration that exports `AddItem` (with all its fields — that's what `(..)` means) and the `decide` function.

**JS analogue:** `export { AddItem, decide } from './MyApp/Cart/Commands/AddItem';`

```haskell
import Core
import Decider qualified
import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)
```

**What you see:** Three imports.

- `import Core` imports everything from `Core` into scope, unqualified.
- `import Decider qualified` imports `Decider` but requires you to call things as `Decider.reject`, `Decider.acceptExisting`, etc. — namespace-prefixed.
- `import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)` imports only `WebTransport` from that module.

**JS analogue:**
```js
import * from 'core';
import * as Decider from 'decider';
import { WebTransport } from 'service/transport/web';
```

```haskell
data AddItem = AddItem
  { cartId :: Uuid
  , stockId :: Uuid
  , quantity :: Int
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show)
```

**What you see:** A record type with three fields. `deriving (Generic, Show)` tells the compiler to auto-generate some boilerplate — you don't have to know what it does yet, just that it's required.

**JS/TS analogue:**
```ts
type AddItem = {
  cartId: string;  // a UUID
  stockId: string;
  quantity: number;
};
```

The field types are on the right side of `::`. Read `cartId :: Uuid` as "cartId has type Uuid."

```haskell
decide :: AddItem -> Maybe CartEntity -> RequestContext -> Decision CartEvent
```

**What you see:** A type signature for a function called `decide`.

**How to read it:** "decide takes an `AddItem`, a `Maybe CartEntity`, a `RequestContext`, and returns a `Decision CartEvent`."

Each `->` separates an argument. The last one is the return type. So this function has three inputs and one output.

**TypeScript equivalent:**
```ts
function decide(
  cmd: AddItem,
  cart: CartEntity | null,
  ctx: RequestContext
): Decision<CartEvent>
```

<Aside type="tip" title="Why is 'Maybe CartEntity' different from 'CartEntity | null'?">
`Maybe` is the explicit "this could be missing" type. It forces you to check for `Nothing` before using the value — the compiler won't let you skip that step. It's the same idea as TypeScript's strict null checks, but always on, always enforced.
</Aside>

```haskell
decide cmd cart _ctx = case cart of
  Nothing ->
    Decider.reject "Cart not found"
  Just c ->
    if cmd.quantity <= 0
      then Decider.reject "Quantity must be positive"
      else
        Decider.acceptExisting
          [ ItemAdded
              { entityId = c.cartId
              , stockId = cmd.stockId
              , quantity = cmd.quantity
              }
          ]
```

**What you see:** The function body. Arguments are listed after the function name (`cmd`, `cart`, `_ctx` — the underscore means "we don't use this one"). Everything after `=` is the value the function returns.

**Read it like this:**
- `case cart of` — switch on whether `cart` is `Nothing` (null) or `Just c` (not null, with the value bound to `c`).
- `Nothing -> Decider.reject "Cart not found"` — if null, reject with a reason.
- `Just c -> if cmd.quantity <= 0 then ... else ...` — if non-null, check the quantity.
- `Decider.acceptExisting [...]` — accept the command and produce a list of events (one in this case).

**JS/TS equivalent:**
```ts
function decide(cmd, cart, _ctx) {
  if (cart === null) {
    return Decider.reject("Cart not found");
  }
  if (cmd.quantity <= 0) {
    return Decider.reject("Quantity must be positive");
  }
  return Decider.acceptExisting([
    {
      kind: "ItemAdded",
      entityId: cart.cartId,
      stockId: cmd.stockId,
      quantity: cmd.quantity,
    },
  ]);
}
```

The logic is identical. NeoHaskell uses `case`/`if`/records the same way TypeScript does. The difference is that the compiler forces you to handle *every* case of `cart`, every case of the event type downstream, every missing field, every type mismatch — before the program runs.

## The pipe operator

You will see `|>` everywhere. It is not magic. It is just function application, written left-to-right instead of inside-out.

```haskell
x |> f |> g |> h
```

Means exactly the same as:

```haskell
h (g (f x))
```

Which in TypeScript is:

```ts
h(g(f(x)))
```

Use whichever reads better. NeoHaskell prefers `|>` because it reads top-down and lines up cleanly in vertical chains:

```haskell
Application.new
  |> Application.withEventStore config
  |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
  |> Application.withService cartService
  |> Application.withQuery @CartSummary
```

Read that as: "Take a new Application. Add an event store. Add a web transport. Add a cart service. Add a query." Each step transforms the value and hands the result to the next step.

**JS equivalent:**
```js
withQuery(
  withService(
    withTransport(
      withEventStore(Application.new, config),
      WebTransport.server
    ),
    cartService
  ),
  CartSummary
);
```

…or with the proposed pipe operator:
```js
Application.new
  |> withEventStore(%, config)
  |> withTransport(%, WebTransport.server)
  |> withService(%, cartService)
  |> withQuery(%, CartSummary);
```

NeoHaskell has had pipes since day one. They are not an afterthought.

## `do` blocks

A `do` block is a sequence of steps inside a `Task`. Each step can be named with `<-` (bind) or just executed for its side effect.

```haskell
handleRequest :: Request -> Task Text Response
handleRequest req = do
  user <- fetchUser req.userId
  cart <- fetchCart user.id
  updatedCart <- addItem cart req.item
  Task.yield (renderResponse updatedCart)
```

**Read it as:**

1. Fetch a user. Bind the result to `user`.
2. Fetch that user's cart. Bind the result to `cart`.
3. Add an item. Bind the result to `updatedCart`.
4. Return a rendered response.

**TypeScript equivalent:**

```ts
async function handleRequest(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await fetchUser(req.userId);
  const cart = await fetchCart(user.id);
  const updatedCart = await addItem(cart, req.item);
  return renderResponse(updatedCart);
}
```

`<-` is `await`. `Task.yield` is `return`. `Task.throw` is `throw`. If any step throws, the whole block short-circuits. That is it. If someone tells you a `do` block is a monad and starts drawing arrows, ignore them — for your purposes, it is async/await.

## Record access

NeoHaskell uses **dot notation** for records, the way nearly every mainstream language does:

```haskell
user.name           -- Get the name field
user.address.city   -- Nested access
```

If you had a variable `cart` of type `CartEntity` with a `cartId` field, you write `cart.cartId`. That is all there is to it.

## Record construction

Creating a record uses the field names explicitly:

```haskell
user = User
  { name = "Alice"
  , email = "alice@example.com"
  , age = 30
  }
```

Notice the commas go at the **start** of each line, not the end. That is a NeoHaskell style convention — it makes adding and removing lines cleaner in diffs.

## Record update

Updating some fields of an existing record looks like this:

```haskell
olderUser = user { age = user.age + 1 }
```

This does not mutate `user`. It creates a *new* record with `age` bumped by one, and leaves `user` alone. NeoHaskell has no mutation in your domain code — every "update" is really "build a new version based on the old one."

## Strings

Plain strings use double quotes:

```haskell
greeting = "Hello, world!"
```

For interpolation, use the `[fmt|...|]` quoter:

```haskell
message = [fmt|Hello, #{name}! You have #{count} unread messages.|]
```

`#{expr}` injects any expression into the string. Think of it as JavaScript's backtick template literals, except instead of `${x}` you write `#{x}`.

<Aside type="note" title="Never use ++ for strings">
You may see `"Hello, " ++ name` in older code or snippets from other places — NeoHaskell style is to use `[fmt|Hello, #{name}|]` instead. It is cleaner, faster, and more explicit.
</Aside>

## The vocabulary you need

You now have enough to read any NeoHaskell file. A few more terms to know — they appear so often that knowing them by name helps:

- **`Uuid`** — a universally unique identifier. Just a string on the wire.
- **`Text`** — a string. Use this, not the older `String`.
- **`Int`** — an integer.
- **`Array`** — an ordered collection. `Array.map`, `Array.filter`, etc.
- **`Map`** — a key-value dictionary. `Map.get`, `Map.set`.
- **`Maybe a`** — either `Just a` (a value) or `Nothing` (no value).
- **`Result err ok`** — either `Ok ok` (success) or `Err err` (failure).
- **`Task err ok`** — an async computation that can succeed with `ok` or fail with `err`.
- **`Decision event`** — what `decide` returns: a request to accept (producing events) or reject (with a reason).

## Try it

Grab any file from [the NeoHaskell testbed](https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/tree/main/testbed/src) and read it. With the dictionary above, you should be able to follow along. If you hit something confusing, jump to the [cheat sheet](/getting-started/cheat-sheet/) for quick reference.

# syntax-warmup.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/getting-started/syntax-warmup.mdx

title: "Syntax warm-up"
description: "Ten short exercises to cement the NeoHaskell building blocks. Records, pattern matching, pipes, do blocks, Maybe, Result."
sidebar:
  order: 4

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You've read about the syntax. Now let's build muscle memory. Work through these ten exercises in order. Each takes about thirty seconds. By the end, the language will feel familiar, not alien.

You can do these in any NeoHaskell module — create a scratch file inside your template project, or use `ghci` from the dev shell if you prefer a REPL.

## Exercise 1 — Define a record

**Goal:** Make a record type for a book.

```haskell
data Book = Book
  { title :: Text
  , author :: Text
  , pages :: Int
  }
  deriving (Show)
```

**Test it:** Construct one.

```haskell
myBook :: Book
myBook = Book
  { title = "The Goal"
  , author = "Eliyahu Goldratt"
  , pages = 384
  }
```

**Key takeaway:** Commas go at the start of each line, not the end. Field names are explicit. `deriving (Show)` lets you print the value for debugging.

## Exercise 2 — Read a field

**Goal:** Get the title of `myBook`.

```haskell
title :: Text
title = myBook.title
```

**Key takeaway:** Dot access, just like JavaScript or Python.

## Exercise 3 — Update a field

**Goal:** Make a copy of `myBook` with one more page.

```haskell
longerBook :: Book
longerBook = myBook { pages = myBook.pages + 1 }
```

**Key takeaway:** Record update creates a new record — it never mutates the original. `myBook` still has its original `pages` value.

## Exercise 4 — Pattern match with `case`

**Goal:** Categorize a book by its page count.

```haskell
sizeLabel :: Book -> Text
sizeLabel book = case book.pages of
  n | n < 100 -> "pamphlet"
  n | n < 300 -> "short"
  n | n < 600 -> "average"
  _ -> "tome"
```

**Key takeaway:** `case` with guards (`|`) is how you express "if this, elif that, else." The underscore `_` catches anything not matched above.

## Exercise 5 — Pipe a value through functions

**Goal:** Take a book title, uppercase it, and trim whitespace.

```haskell
import Text qualified

cleanTitle :: Book -> Text
cleanTitle book =
  book.title
    |> Text.trim
    |> Text.toUpper
```

**Key takeaway:** `|>` reads left-to-right. `book.title` is the value, `Text.trim` transforms it, `Text.toUpper` transforms the result of that. You can read this as "take the title, trim it, then uppercase it."

## Exercise 6 — Work with `Maybe`

**Goal:** Write a function that returns the first character of a title, or `Nothing` if the title is empty.

```haskell
import Maybe qualified
import Text qualified

firstLetter :: Text -> Maybe Char
firstLetter text = case Text.uncons text of
  Nothing -> Nothing
  Just (c, _) -> Just c
```

**Test it:**

```haskell
firstLetter "NeoHaskell"  -- Just 'N'
firstLetter ""            -- Nothing
```

**Key takeaway:** `Maybe` forces you to think about "what if it's missing?" The compiler will not let you skip the `Nothing` case.

## Exercise 7 — Work with `Result`

**Goal:** Parse an integer from text, returning either `Ok n` or `Err reason`.

```haskell
import Int qualified

parseAge :: Text -> Result Text Int
parseAge text = case Int.fromText text of
  Nothing -> Err "not a valid integer"
  Just n -> if n < 0
    then Err "age cannot be negative"
    else Ok n
```

**Test it:**

```haskell
parseAge "42"    -- Ok 42
parseAge "-3"    -- Err "age cannot be negative"
parseAge "hello" -- Err "not a valid integer"
```

**Key takeaway:** `Result err ok` expresses "this might fail, and here's why." Unlike exceptions, failures are part of the type — you have to handle them.

## Exercise 8 — A sum type

**Goal:** Model a traffic light with three colors.

```haskell
data Light
  = Red
  | Yellow
  | Green
  deriving (Eq, Show)

nextLight :: Light -> Light
nextLight light = case light of
  Red -> Green
  Green -> Yellow
  Yellow -> Red
```

**Key takeaway:** This is the most basic sum type — three variants with no fields. The compiler will reject `nextLight` if you miss a case. Try commenting out one branch and watch it scream.

## Exercise 9 — A sum type with fields

**Goal:** Model a payment event that can be a deposit or a withdrawal, each with an amount.

```haskell
data PaymentEvent
  = Deposited { amount :: Int }
  | Withdrawn { amount :: Int }
  deriving (Show)

describe :: PaymentEvent -> Text
describe event = case event of
  Deposited { amount } -> [fmt|Deposited $#{amount}|]
  Withdrawn { amount } -> [fmt|Withdrew $#{amount}|]
```

**Test it:**

```haskell
describe (Deposited { amount = 50 })  -- "Deposited $50"
describe (Withdrawn { amount = 20 })  -- "Withdrew $20"
```

**Key takeaway:** Sum types with record fields are how you describe "one of several different shapes of data." Every event type in NeoHaskell looks like this. Fold over them with `case`.

## Exercise 10 — A `do` block

**Goal:** Write a task that reads a name from the console and prints a greeting.

```haskell
import Console qualified

greet :: Task Text Unit
greet = do
  Console.print "What is your name?"
  name <- Console.readLine
  Console.print [fmt|Hello, #{name}!|]
```

**Key takeaway:** `do` blocks sequence steps. `<-` captures a value from a step that returns something. Steps without `<-` are run for their effect. This is async/await with a different name.

## Quick reference — the moves you just learned

| Move | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Define a record | `data Foo = Foo { a :: Int, b :: Text }` |
| Construct a record | `Foo { a = 1, b = "x" }` |
| Read a field | `foo.a` |
| Update a field | `foo { a = 42 }` |
| Pattern match | `case x of ...` |
| Pipe | `x \|> f \|> g` |
| Maybe | `Just x` or `Nothing` |
| Result | `Ok x` or `Err reason` |
| Sum type | `data Light = Red \| Yellow \| Green` |
| Do block | `do { x <- step1; step2 x }` |
| String interpolation | `[fmt\|hello #{name}\|]` |

That is the entire vocabulary you need for the tutorial. If any of these feel shaky, re-read the exercise — muscle memory is about repetition, not complexity.

## What's next

You know how to read NeoHaskell. You know how to write the basic moves. You're ready for the real thing.

- [**Build NeoBank**](/tutorial/) — the tutorial that teaches you the full language by building a banking service.
- [**Your first events**](/getting-started/first-events/) — if you want one more small warm-up before the tutorial.
- [**Cheat sheet**](/getting-started/cheat-sheet/) — one-page reference for when you forget a syntax.

# NeoHaskell coding rules

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/getting-started/using-ai.mdx

title: "Using AI with NeoHaskell"
description: "NeoHaskell is built for AI-assisted development. A ready-to-paste system prompt, the common drift to watch for, and why the compiler makes smaller, cheaper AI models actually work."
sidebar:
  order: 5

import { Aside, Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Most software is written with AI assistance now. That is reality, not a problem. NeoHaskell was designed with this reality in mind, and the fit is unusually tight: the language's rules happen to be exactly the rules AI assistants are bad at enforcing on their own.

This page covers what that means in practice — the workflow, the ready-to-paste system prompt, and the reason you can get by with cheaper models in NeoHaskell than you can anywhere else.

## Why NeoHaskell is good for AI-assisted development

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Wrong code does not compile" icon="approve-check">
    The compiler enforces every event-sourcing contract. If the assistant forgets a case, uses the wrong type, mismatches an event, or misconfigures a service, the build fails with a specific error. You learn within seconds, not in production.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Less code per feature" icon="document">
    Commands, events, entities, and queries are language primitives — there is no glue layer for the assistant to hallucinate. A command handler is one pure function. A query is one pure function. The assistant cannot invent a fictional middleware layer because there is no middleware layer to invent.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Context windows go further" icon="puzzle">
    Small files, a curated standard library, and zero boilerplate mean the assistant can hold entire modules in its working memory. Fewer hallucinations happen when the model can see the types it needs to match.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Cheaper models work" icon="seti:shell">
    You do not need a frontier model to write correct NeoHaskell. The compiler is the validator — a smaller, faster, cheaper model produces output that either compiles (and is structurally correct) or fails a check the assistant itself can fix. Token spend drops accordingly.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

The important claim is the last one, and it is worth sitting with for a moment. In a loose language, the quality of your AI-assisted code is roughly proportional to the quality of your model — because the model is the only thing enforcing correctness. In NeoHaskell, the compiler is the enforcer, and the model's job shrinks to "propose something plausible." Plausible code that does not satisfy the contract does not ship; it fails the build. The assistant reads the error and tries again. You stop paying for a giant model to catch mistakes a smaller one would miss.

## The AI loop that actually works

Here is the workflow. This is not hypothetical — it is the shape you'll settle into within a day of using an assistant with NeoHaskell:

1. **You describe what you want** in plain language. One command, one query, one feature at a time.
2. **The assistant writes the code** following the NeoHaskell conventions (from the system prompt below).
3. **You run `cabal build`**. If it compiles, the assistant's code is structurally correct — every event handled, every type matched, every service consistent.
4. **If it does not compile**, you paste the error back to the assistant verbatim. Errors in NeoHaskell are specific enough that the assistant usually fixes them in one round.
5. **You run `cabal test`**. Pure function tests are fast and trivial for the assistant to write. They catch the logic bugs the compiler can't.

The loop is tight because the feedback is immediate. The assistant is not guessing about whether its output is correct — the build tells it. You are not reviewing output line by line — the compiler already did.

<Aside type="note" title="The 'regenerate until it works' anti-pattern">
In looser languages, the default AI workflow is "regenerate until it compiles, ship it, hope the tests pass." That only works when the compiler is weak enough that "compiles" doesn't mean much. In NeoHaskell, "compiles" is a meaningful guarantee — it means the structural contracts hold. You do fewer regenerate rounds, you write fewer throwaway tests, and you ship with more confidence.
</Aside>

## Ready-to-paste system prompt

Paste this into your assistant's rules file — Cursor's `.cursorrules`, Claude Code's `CLAUDE.md`, Copilot instructions, OpenCode's `AGENTS.md`, or whatever your tool uses. It contains everything the assistant needs to write idiomatic NeoHaskell on the first try.

````markdown
# NeoHaskell coding rules

You are writing NeoHaskell. NeoHaskell is a strongly-typed, purely functional
language where event sourcing, commands, queries, entities, services, and
integrations are first-class primitives. The compiler enforces every contract.
Follow these rules exactly — they are not style preferences, they are how the
language is used.

## Core rules

- Use `|>` for function application. Never `$`, never nested parentheses.
- Use `do` blocks for anything inside a `Task`. `<-` is `await`,
  `Task.yield` is `return`, `Task.throw` is `throw`.
- Use `case ... of` for pattern matching. Never pattern-match in function
  definitions.
- Use `let` inside `do` blocks for local bindings. Never `let ... in`.
  Never `where`.
- Use `[fmt|Hello #{name}|]` for string interpolation. Never `++` for strings.
- Commas go at the START of each line in records and lists.
- Use descriptive type variable names (`forall input output.`), not single
  letters.
- Use qualified imports (`import Text qualified`). Only `import Core` is
  unqualified.

## Types

- `Task err val` — async/effectful computation with a typed error channel.
  Use this instead of `IO a`.
- `Result err ok` — pure computation that can fail. Use instead of `Either`.
- `Text` — strict UTF-8 text. Use instead of `String`.
- `Array a` — efficient persistent sequence. Use for user-facing collections.
- `Map k v` — immutable key-value map.
- `Maybe a` — optional value (`Nothing` or `Just x`).
- `Uuid` — universal identifier.

## Return values

- `Task.yield value` — return inside a `Task`. Never `pure`, never `return`.
- `Task.throw err` — fail inside a `Task`.
- `Ok value` / `Err reason` — for `Result`.

## Event sourcing primitives (the most important rules)

- Commands have a pure `decide` function:
  `decide :: Command -> Maybe Entity -> RequestContext -> Decision Event`
- `decide` returns one of:
  - `Decider.acceptNew [events]` (stream must not exist)
  - `Decider.acceptExisting [events]` (stream must exist)
  - `Decider.acceptAfter position [events]` (optimistic concurrency)
  - `Decider.reject "reason"` (business rule violation)
- Entities implement `class Entity` with `initialStateImpl` and `updateImpl`.
- Events implement `class Event` with `getEventEntityIdImpl`.
- The `update` function must handle every event variant. This is enforced
  by the compiler — missing cases are compile errors.
- Services are built with `Service.new |> Service.command @Foo |> ...`.
  All commands in a service MUST share the same entity and event type.
- Applications are built with `Application.new |> Application.withEventStore
  ... |> Application.withService ... |> Application.withQuery @Foo |> ...`.

## Forbidden patterns

- Never use `IO a`. Use `Task err val`.
- Never use `Either`. Use `Result`.
- Never use `pure` or `return`. Use `Task.yield`.
- Never use `let ... in`. Use `let` inside `do`, or a top-level helper.
- Never use `where` clauses. Use top-level helpers or `let` inside `do`.
- Never use `++` for strings. Use `[fmt|...|]`.
- Never use point-free style.
- Never use monad transformers (`StateT`, `ReaderT`, etc.).
- Never use code-generation macros except the four provided helpers:
  `command ''Foo`, `deriveQuery ''Q [''E]`, `defineConfig "Name" [...]`,
  and the `[fmt|...|]` string interpolation quoter.
- Never pattern-match in a function head. Use `case`.
- Never import from `base` without prefixing with `Ghc`
  (`import Data.List qualified as GhcList`).

## File layout

- `src/MyApp/Feature/Core.hs` — entity and events.
- `src/MyApp/Feature/Commands/DoThing.hs` — one command per file.
- `src/MyApp/Feature/Queries/FeatureSummary.hs` — one query per file.
- `src/MyApp/Feature/Integrations/Reactor.hs` — one integration per file.
- `src/MyApp/Feature/Service.hs` — assembles commands into a Service.

## Verification

After generating any code:

1. State which compile-time checks will run on it
   (pattern exhaustiveness, event-type consistency, transport registration).
2. State what error messages to expect if something is wrong.
3. If asked to write a command, also write a Given-When-Then test for it.

## The compiler is the validator

If your output compiles with `cabal build`, it is structurally correct —
every event is handled, every type matches, every service is consistent.
If the user pastes an error back to you, read the first line of the error
(the summary) and fix exactly what it names. Do not rewrite unrelated code.
````

This prompt is long but specific. It covers nearly every drift that assistants fall into. Save it, paste it, forget about it.

## Common drift, and how to catch it

Even with the system prompt above, assistants sometimes slip. Here are the most common drifts and the quickest way to spot each one.

### 1. Using `IO` instead of `Task`

Other strongly-typed functional languages use `IO a` for effectful computations. NeoHaskell uses `Task err val`. If the assistant writes:

```haskell
-- Wrong
fetchUser :: Uuid -> IO User
```

Correct it to:

```haskell
-- Right
fetchUser :: Uuid -> Task Text User
```

**How to spot it:** Search for `:: IO ` in any generated file. Replace with `Task <error> <value>`.

### 2. Using `pure` or `return`

```haskell
-- Wrong
fetchUser userId = do
  user <- lookupUser userId
  pure user

-- Right
fetchUser userId = do
  user <- lookupUser userId
  Task.yield user
```

**How to spot it:** Search for `pure ` or `return ` on their own line. Replace with `Task.yield`.

### 3. Using `++` for string concatenation

```haskell
-- Wrong
greet name = "Hello, " ++ name ++ "!"

-- Right
greet name = [fmt|Hello, #{name}!|]
```

**How to spot it:** Search for `++`. For lists, `++` is fine — for text, use `fmt`.

### 4. Using `let ... in`

```haskell
-- Wrong
total = let subtotal = price * qty
            tax = subtotal * 0.1
        in subtotal + tax

-- Right (inside a do block)
total = do
  let subtotal = price * qty
  let tax = subtotal * 0.1
  Task.yield (subtotal + tax)
```

**How to spot it:** Search for `let` followed by `in` on the same or adjacent lines.

### 5. Pattern matching in the function head

```haskell
-- Wrong
handle (Just user) = greet user
handle Nothing = Task.throw "no user"

-- Right
handle maybeUser = case maybeUser of
  Just user -> greet user
  Nothing -> Task.throw "no user"
```

**How to spot it:** Look for multiple lines with the same function name but different argument shapes. Rewrite as a single function with a `case`.

## Reducing token spend

One of the less obvious benefits of NeoHaskell with AI: you use fewer tokens, both per request and per feature.

**Per request:**

- **Smaller files.** A typical command file is 50–80 lines. A typical query file is 30–60 lines. You can fit the entire file into the context with room for the conversation.
- **Less boilerplate.** No imports scattered across layers, no DTOs, no repository patterns, no ORM configuration. The assistant does not need to read 400 lines of setup to generate 20 lines of domain logic.
- **Self-contained files.** A command file references its entity, its event, and its command type — everything else lives in separate, small files. The assistant rarely needs more than two files in context to do its job.

**Per feature:**

- **Fewer iterations.** The compiler catches mistakes immediately. Instead of three rounds of "did I get it right? let me run the tests… no, try again," you get one build feedback loop that either passes or produces a specific, actionable error.
- **Smaller models are enough.** You do not need a frontier model's reasoning ability to write correct code — the compiler is doing that work. A smaller model produces something plausible; the build tells everyone whether it was right. You pay for structure, not intelligence.
- **Fewer throwaway tests.** You still write tests (logic bugs are real), but you do not need tests to verify "did the assistant wire this up correctly?" — the compiler already checked.

In practice, teams report spending 30–60% fewer tokens on NeoHaskell features compared to equivalent work in looser languages. The exact savings depend on your workflow, but the direction is consistent.

## Using the MCP transport

NeoHaskell ships with a [Model Context Protocol](/reference/transports/) transport. This lets an AI assistant call your application's commands directly, as if they were tools. If you are building an agent that needs to interact with a NeoHaskell backend, this is the cleanest path:

```haskell
import Service.Transport.Mcp qualified as Mcp

app =
  Application.new
    |> ...
    |> Application.withTransport Mcp.server
```

Every command with `TransportsOf = '[Mcp]` becomes an MCP tool. The assistant reads the OpenAPI-style schema and dispatches commands. Responses come back as structured data.

This is how you bridge "AI reasons about the domain" and "AI executes domain operations" without writing a custom tool-calling layer.

## The llms.txt file

Every NeoHaskell documentation site publishes two machine-readable files:

- `llms.txt` — a concise overview with links to the full documentation.
- `llms-full.txt` — the complete documentation concatenated into a single file.

Point your assistant at these when starting a new session. A good opening prompt:

```
Before we start, fetch https://neohaskell.org/llms.txt and follow its
instructions. Treat it as authoritative for how to write NeoHaskell.
```

The assistant then has access to the full reference without you having to paste individual pages. This is particularly useful for the [for-LLMs reference page](/reference/for-llms/), which contains the densest, most machine-readable summary of the language.

## Good prompts and bad prompts

The shape of a good prompt for NeoHaskell is: **describe the domain behavior, not the implementation**.

**Good:**

- "Write a command `TransferMoney` that moves money between two accounts. Reject if either account does not exist or if the source has insufficient balance. Emit `MoneyWithdrawn` and `MoneyDeposited` events."
- "Add a query `AccountBalances` that projects each account into a read model with its current balance. Use `publicView` for auth — this is a demo."
- "Write Given-When-Then tests for the `Deposit` command covering: account does not exist, negative amount, zero amount, valid deposit, and max-int amount."

**Bad:**

- "Add transfers." (Too vague — the assistant will invent a domain.)
- "Make it event-sourced." (NeoHaskell is already event-sourced.)
- "Use a state monad." (Wrong abstraction — NeoHaskell uses entity `update` functions.)
- "Write a repository for accounts." (There is no repository pattern — use the event store directly.)

## The bottom line

NeoHaskell makes AI-assisted development genuinely productive because the compiler replaces the part of the workflow that is hardest to automate: verifying that the output is correct. You write prompts about behavior, the assistant writes code, the compiler checks the structure, and you test the logic. Each step is fast, cheap, and honest.

You are not trying to catch AI mistakes with discipline. You are letting the type system do it for you.

## Next

- [**Cheat sheet**](/getting-started/cheat-sheet/) — keep it open when you are reviewing assistant output.
- [**Reference → For LLMs**](/reference/for-llms/) — the densest machine-readable summary of the language.
- [**Build NeoBank**](/tutorial/) — the tutorial. Try it with your assistant as a pair-programming partner.

# adopting-at-work.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/adopting-at-work.mdx

title: "Adopting NeoHaskell at work"
description: "A pragmatic guide to introducing NeoHaskell at your company — proposal templates, objection responses, pilot strategies, and success metrics."
sidebar:
  order: 9

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This is the guide you want if you just finished the tutorial, you're convinced, and now you have to explain this decision to the rest of your team. Enthusiasm is not a plan. This page is the plan.

Adopting a new language is rarely a technical problem — it's an organizational problem. The code works. The real questions are: will the team learn it? Will we be able to hire? What if the champion leaves? What if it turns out to be the wrong call? Addressing those questions honestly is what makes an adoption stick.

## Step 1 — Be honest with yourself about fit

Before you pitch NeoHaskell to anyone, check the [trade-offs](/concepts/trade-offs/) page and the [architecture evaluation](/concepts/architecture-evaluation/). Answer these questions for yourself first:

- Does our domain genuinely benefit from event sourcing? If not, NeoHaskell is over-engineering.
- Do we have at least one engineer (ideally two) willing to learn it deeply?
- Do we have the organizational appetite for a slower first month in exchange for a faster long-term pace?
- What will we do if the maintainers of NeoHaskell disappear in a year?

If you can't answer these confidently, don't pitch it yet. Do a weekend project first, validate your own conviction, then come back.

## Step 2 — Pick a pilot project

The single biggest factor in a successful adoption is the pilot project. Pick badly and you'll spend months fighting. Pick well and you'll have a reference everyone can point to.

### Ideal pilot characteristics

- **New feature, not a rewrite.** Rewriting an existing system means you're fighting the old one and the new language at the same time. A new feature lets NeoHaskell succeed on its own merits.
- **Clearly bounded.** The smaller and more independent the better. "Add a new microservice" is easier than "rewrite the checkout flow."
- **Domain-rich.** NeoHaskell shines when there are interesting state transitions. A settings panel is a bad pilot. An order management service is a good one.
- **Non-critical, but visible.** If the pilot fails, the business doesn't suffer. If it succeeds, people notice.
- **Has a clear success metric.** "Fewer bugs in production", "faster feature delivery", "better audit capability" — pick one and measure it.

### Anti-patterns

- **The "rewrite everything" pilot.** Never. Always additive.
- **The "tiny CRUD endpoint" pilot.** Doesn't show the benefits of NeoHaskell; people come away thinking "that was a lot of work for a simple feature."
- **The "mission-critical" pilot.** If it fails, the damage is catastrophic. Start lower stakes.
- **The "nobody needs this" pilot.** If nobody cares about the feature, success doesn't buy you political capital.

## Step 3 — Write a proposal

You need something written down. A proposal for engineering leadership should cover:

1. **The problem.** What's the specific pain point NeoHaskell solves for us? Be concrete — "we've had three incidents in the last year where state was inconsistent across services and we couldn't reconstruct the history" is much better than "we want better types."
2. **The proposal.** "We pilot NeoHaskell for [specific feature] with [specific engineer(s)] over [specific timeline]."
3. **The investment.** Engineering time, training, tooling setup.
4. **The success criteria.** What outcomes would justify broader adoption? What would trigger a rollback?
5. **The rollback plan.** If the pilot fails, how do we unwind it without wasting the work?
6. **The FAQ.** Preempt the objections. The next section is the material for this.

Keep the proposal to two pages. Executives read the summary and the FAQ. Detail goes in appendices.

## Step 4 — Preempt the objections

Here are the objections you will hear, and honest responses.

### "Who will maintain this after you leave?"

**Response:** "Any engineer who can read Go or Python can learn NeoHaskell in a few weeks. The [tutorial](/tutorial/) gets them productive, and the [concept pages](/concepts/) teach the mental model. If I leave, the next engineer will ramp up faster than on any legacy codebase because the code is smaller and the compiler catches most mistakes."

### "We can't hire NeoHaskell developers."

**Response:** "We don't need to. We hire generalists and train them — the same way we'd train someone on our internal frameworks, except the training materials are better. The relevant skill is thinking in events, and that transfers from any language."

### "What if NeoHaskell is abandoned?"

**Response:** "It compiles to native code via GHC, which is a production-grade compiler with decades of history. If the NeoHaskell project stagnates, we can keep running the code we have indefinitely. If we need to add new features, we can fork it. It's open-source and the code is approachable."

### "Functional programming is too hard for our team."

**Response:** "The code we'll write looks like this [show a `decide` function from the tutorial]. It has `case`, `if`, records, and pipes. No monads, no category theory, no academic jargon in our application code. Any developer who has written a Redux reducer has the skills."

### "We already have patterns for event sourcing in [X]. Why switch?"

**Response:** "We have patterns, but the compiler doesn't enforce them. In NeoHaskell, breaking the event-sourcing contract is a compile error, not a runtime one. That's the difference between 'we have a convention' and 'the convention is a type.'"

### "This will slow us down in the short term."

**Response:** "Yes, for about a month. After that, we'll be faster than before because the compiler catches mistakes that currently become production incidents. The pilot project's metrics will tell us whether the tradeoff holds."

### "We can't afford to experiment."

**Response:** "We also can't afford to keep fighting the same class of bugs. The pilot is bounded — one feature, one timeline, clear success criteria. If it doesn't work, we spent a month; if it does, we learned how to build more reliable systems."

## Step 5 — Run the pilot

During the pilot, some habits that help:

### Over-communicate

Send a weekly update to your engineering org. Include:

- What shipped.
- What surprised you (good and bad).
- What you learned.
- What's next.

Short, specific, regular. People trust work they can see. Missing updates breed suspicion.

### Write down the lessons

Keep a living document of "things we learned about NeoHaskell that surprised us." This becomes your internal onboarding doc when you expand.

### Benchmark against the alternative

If the pilot replaces something that would have been built in another language, keep track of the "alternate history" — how many lines of code, how many bugs, how much test coverage. When you pitch broader adoption, these numbers will matter.

### Pair with skeptics

Invite your most skeptical teammate to pair-program on the pilot. Either they'll become your second champion, or you'll learn about objections you hadn't considered. Both outcomes are good.

### Don't sell it internally until you're ready

Early in the pilot, focus on making the pilot work. Resist the urge to evangelize until you have something compelling to show. Early evangelism with unfinished work creates headwinds.

## Step 6 — Evaluate honestly

At the end of the pilot:

- Did it meet the success criteria?
- Did it cost more or less than you expected?
- What surprised you?
- What would you do differently next time?
- Would the team be comfortable continuing in NeoHaskell?

Write it up honestly. If the pilot failed, say so. A failed pilot that you can explain is better than a "success" that nobody believes.

## Step 7 — Expand or unwind

If the pilot succeeded:

1. **Present the results** to engineering leadership.
2. **Propose the next project.** Don't try to convert everything at once; pick another bounded feature.
3. **Train a second champion.** Someone who's not you.
4. **Document conventions.** As you adopt more of the language, write down the patterns that work and the ones that don't.
5. **Grow incrementally.** Six months of gradual adoption beats one big-bang switch.

If the pilot failed:

1. **Document why.** Was it the language, the problem, the team, the timing? Be specific.
2. **Unwind carefully.** The feature you built needs to keep running (or be rewritten in your usual stack). Don't let the "pilot" code become orphaned tech debt.
3. **Share the lessons.** A failed pilot is a learning opportunity for the org. Treat it that way.

## A realistic timeline

For a team of 2–3 engineers working on the pilot part-time (not full-time, not AI-assisted, writing everything by hand):

- **Week 1:** Installation, template setup, tutorial completion for the pilot team.
- **Week 2:** First few commands and queries written. Productive but slow.
- **Week 3:** Feature feels "small enough" that the team is confident shipping.
- **Week 4:** First feature deployed to a canary environment.
- **Weeks 5–8:** Iterate, fix bugs, learn the edge cases. Feature running in production.
- **Weeks 9–12:** Second feature, often 2x faster than the first.
- **Month 4+:** Consider expanding. The team should feel comfortable picking up NeoHaskell work without friction.

If someone on the team is working full-time with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.), expect roughly 3–5x compression on those timelines. The compiler validates the assistant's output, so the ramp is less about "learn the syntax" and more about "learn the domain modeling." A full-time, AI-assisted engineer typically ships the first feature in week 1 and hits full stride by week 3. The tutorial takes an afternoon instead of a week because the assistant handles the boilerplate while the engineer focuses on understanding the patterns.

## When to stop trying

Some adoptions don't stick. Signs that it's time to step back:

- After the pilot, the team is still not comfortable working in NeoHaskell. This is OK — not every team has the interest.
- Leadership won't commit to broader adoption even after a successful pilot. This is usually organizational, not technical.
- You, the champion, have left the company (or plan to). Adoption that depends on one person rarely survives.

If any of these happen, the honest answer is to wind down the NeoHaskell work and continue in your usual stack. Keep the experience — it's valuable for the next team, the next company, or the next problem.

## The bottom line

NeoHaskell adoption is about **earning trust incrementally**. A great pilot earns the right to a second project. A second success earns the right to a standard. You don't get that trust by evangelizing — you get it by shipping something that demonstrably works better than the alternative.

Pick a pilot you can win. Ship it. Measure. Expand.

## Where to go from here

- **[Architecture evaluation](/concepts/architecture-evaluation/)** — the technical tradeoffs in more depth.
- **[Integrating existing systems](/guides/integrating-existing-systems/)** — how to coexist with legacy code during the transition.
- **[Deployment](/guides/deployment/)** — operational concerns when the pilot goes to production.

# Container Apps / Kubernetes-style probes

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server.mdx

title: "Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server"
description: "The golden path for running a NeoHaskell app on Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server behind Container Apps: env-only connection config, the direct-5432 rule, the B1ms connection budget, TLS hardening, scale-to-zero pairing, and storage cost."
sidebar:
  order: 7

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This is the deployment we run for real client projects: one NeoHaskell container on **Azure Container Apps**, talking to one **Azure Database for PostgreSQL — Flexible Server** on the cheap **Burstable `B1ms`** tier. It is the cheapest setup that still survives maintenance restarts and failovers without losing events.

The best part: **connecting NeoHaskell to Flexible Server takes zero code change.** Everything below is configuration. You set some environment variables, you follow one load-bearing rule about ports, and you size the database so it doesn't run out of connections. That's the whole job.

This guide is the runbook. If you just want the moving parts, start with [the short version](#the-short-version); if you're standing up a new client, read it top to bottom once.

## The short version

1. Create a Flexible Server on the `B1ms` tier and a database inside it.
2. Point NeoHaskell at it with environment variables — `DB_HOST`, `DB_PORT`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_NAME`.
3. **Connect on the direct port `5432`. Never the pooler on `6432`.** (See [the direct-5432 rule](#the-direct-5432-rule) — this one is load-bearing.)
4. Leave the database **always-on**. Your app scales to zero; the database does not wake itself up.
5. Optionally harden TLS with `DB_SSL_MODE=require`.
6. Keep an eye on storage growth and backup retention so the bill doesn't surprise you.

## Why Flexible Server

Flexible Server is first-party Azure PostgreSQL. NeoHaskell's event store *is* PostgreSQL (see the [PostgreSQL event store guide](/guides/postgresql-event-store/)), so this is the natural fit:

- **It's real Postgres.** NeoHaskell speaks the Postgres wire protocol. Flexible Server speaks the Postgres wire protocol. Nothing in your application code changes — the same binary that runs against your local `docker compose` Postgres runs against Flexible Server.
- **`B1ms` is cheap.** The Burstable tier is built for workloads that are quiet most of the time and occasionally busy — exactly the shape of a small per-client app. It's the baseline we standardize on.
- **It keeps `LISTEN/NOTIFY`.** NeoHaskell's live projections and integrations are driven by Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`. Flexible Server supports it natively. (The alternatives — Azure SQL, Cosmos DB — don't, which would mean a data-layer rewrite that also regresses correctness. Flexible Server wins on every lens.)

<Aside type="note" title="Why not a managed connection pooler or a serverless SQL?">
The whole point of NeoHaskell on Postgres is that you don't rewrite anything. A NoSQL or T-SQL backend would be cheaper at idle but would cost you `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, a Haskell driver, and portability. Burstable `B1ms` keeps all three for a few dollars a month.
</Aside>

## Connecting: environment variables only

NeoHaskell reads its database configuration from environment variables. There is no connection string to assemble and no code to edit. Here are the variables your app reads (these are the real names — they come straight from the testbed's config):

{/* source: neohaskell/neohaskell/testbed/src/Testbed/Config.hs@2a45427 */}

| Variable | What it is | Default | For Flexible Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DB_HOST` | Database host | `localhost` | `<your-server>.postgres.database.azure.com` |
| `DB_PORT` | Database port | `5432` | `5432` — **the direct port, see below** |
| `DB_USER` | Username | `neohaskell` | your admin or app user |
| `DB_PASSWORD` | Password (secret) | `neohaskell` | from a real secret store |
| `DB_NAME` | Database name | `neohaskell` | the database you created |
| `DB_POOL_SIZE` | EventStore pool size | `6` | leave at `6` on `B1ms` |
| `DB_SSL_MODE` | TLS mode | `unset` | `require` (optional, recommended) |
| `DB_SSL_ROOT_CERT` | CA bundle path | _(empty)_ | only for `verify-full` |

A complete launch command looks like this:

```bash
DB_HOST=myclient-db.postgres.database.azure.com \
DB_PORT=5432 \
DB_USER=appuser \
DB_PASSWORD=$(az keyvault secret show --vault-name myclient-kv --name db-password --query value -o tsv) \
DB_NAME=myclient \
DB_SSL_MODE=require \
HTTP_PORT=8080 \
./your-app
```

On Container Apps you'd set these as environment variables (and the password as a secret reference) in the container app's configuration instead of on the command line. The names are identical.

<Aside type="tip" title="Localhost still works with nothing set">
Every one of these has a sensible default. Running locally against `docker compose` Postgres needs no database config at all — the defaults point at `localhost`. The Flexible Server values are what you add **only** when you deploy.
</Aside>

## The direct-5432 rule

This is the one rule you cannot get wrong.

<Aside type="danger" title="Always connect on 5432. Never the pooler on 6432.">
Flexible Server's General Purpose and Memory Optimized tiers ship a built-in **PgBouncer** connection pooler on port **`6432`**. PgBouncer in its default *transaction* mode **silently breaks `LISTEN/NOTIFY`** — the notifications NeoHaskell relies on to drive live projections and integrations never arrive.

The failure is silent. Your app starts, commands succeed, events are stored — but live projections stop updating and outbound integrations stop firing, with no error and no log line. Always set `DB_PORT=5432` (the **direct** endpoint).
</Aside>

The good news on `B1ms`: **the Burstable tier has no PgBouncer at all**, so the only port available is the direct `5432`. You get the right behavior automatically. The rule matters the moment you upgrade to a General Purpose or Memory Optimized tier (where the pooler exists and is tempting) — keep `DB_PORT=5432` and leave the `6432` pooler switched off.

NeoHaskell already manages its own connection pools (next section), so you are not giving up pooling by skipping PgBouncer — you're keeping the pooling that works with `LISTEN/NOTIFY` and dropping the one that breaks it.

## The connection budget on B1ms

`B1ms` is small. It allows **50 total connections**, of which roughly **15 are reserved** for Azure's superuser, replication, and maintenance — leaving about **35 usable**. A single NeoHaskell app has to fit inside that 35, and it opens connections from several places.

Here's the full budget (the numbers are the shipped defaults):

```text
  EventStore pool        6   (DB_POOL_SIZE, default 6)
  QueryObjectStore pool  4
  FileUpload pool        6   (shares the EventStore pool size)
  ----------------------- 
  pooled subtotal       16

  Listener pair          2   (persistent LISTEN/NOTIFY connections)
  Init-listen            1   (transient, during startup)
  ----------------------- 
  fixed overhead         3

  Per-stream subscription  1 each, while subscribed
  ----------------------- 
  steady-state total    19 + (number of active stream subscriptions)
```

With no stream subscriptions, a NeoHaskell app uses **19 of the 35** usable connections. That leaves about **16** for active stream subscriptions, an operator `psql` session, and a maintenance task.

<Aside type="caution" title="Keep concurrent stream subscriptions bounded on B1ms">
Each active per-stream subscription holds **one** dedicated connection for as long as it's subscribed. On `B1ms`, keep concurrent stream subscriptions to **around 14** so you stay clear of the 35-usable ceiling with headroom for `psql` and maintenance. NeoHaskell releases each subscription's connection on unsubscribe, so well-behaved subscribe/unsubscribe cycles don't accumulate connections — but a lot of *simultaneously open* subscriptions will. If you need more, move up a tier.
</Aside>

If you exceed the ceiling, Postgres rejects new connections with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved` — an outage, not a slowdown. So the budget is a hard limit, not a guideline.

**Raising the budget for a bigger tier.** `DB_POOL_SIZE` tunes the EventStore pool (and, because it shares that config, the FileUpload pool). Moving to **B2s** or a **General Purpose** tier raises `max_connections`, so you can raise `DB_POOL_SIZE` and run more concurrent subscriptions. The rule of thumb: raise the EventStore pool first, since command appends, entity fetches, and query catch-up reads all flow through it.

<Aside type="note" title="Why restarts don't lose events">
A `B1ms` maintenance restart or failover drops the `LISTEN/NOTIFY` connections. NeoHaskell reconnects and does a **position-based catch-up read** — it replays from the last processed position before resuming live dispatch, so events inserted during the outage are *not* silently skipped. You don't have to configure anything for this; it's why Flexible Server's regular restarts are safe.
</Aside>

## TLS hardening (optional, recommended)

You don't *need* TLS config to connect — libpq's default already negotiates TLS against Flexible Server. The reason to set a mode is to **forbid a silent downgrade**: with the default, a stripped or misconfigured negotiation can quietly fall back to plaintext, sending your password and event data unencrypted with no error.

Two modes are worth knowing. Both are off by default, so localhost and dev are completely unaffected.

### `require` — forbid the downgrade

```bash
DB_SSL_MODE=require
```

This makes every NeoHaskell Postgres connection refuse to proceed unencrypted. A downgrade attempt fails loudly at connect time instead of leaking plaintext. This is the recommended baseline for any production deploy — one variable, no certificates to manage.

### `verify-full` — also authenticate the server

```bash
DB_SSL_MODE=verify-full
DB_SSL_ROOT_CERT=/etc/postgresql/azure-roots.pem
```

This adds protection against an active man-in-the-middle: libpq verifies the server's certificate chains to a trusted root **and** that the hostname matches. You supply a CA bundle containing the roots Azure uses:

- **DigiCert Global Root G2**
- **Microsoft RSA Root CA 2017**

<Aside type="caution" title="Root certificates only — never an intermediate or the server cert">
Put **only the root CAs** in your bundle. Microsoft rotates Flexible Server's *intermediate* certificates on an ongoing basis, so pinning an intermediate or the server certificate would break your connection the next time they rotate. Roots are stable; trust those and let the chain validate normally.
</Aside>

<Aside type="danger" title="Never set a client certificate">
Azure Database for PostgreSQL has **no mutual-TLS support**. There is deliberately no client-certificate option in NeoHaskell — supplying `sslcert`/`sslkey` would *break* the connection, not harden it. `DB_SSL_ROOT_CERT` is a server-authentication bundle only.
</Aside>

The mode applies uniformly to **every** Postgres connection NeoHaskell opens — the EventStore pool, the QueryObjectStore pool, the FileUpload pool, and the `LISTEN/NOTIFY` connections. You set it once; you can't accidentally harden one pool and forget another.

## Pairing with Container Apps scale-to-zero

The cheap Container Apps setup runs with `minReplicas=0`: when no requests come in, your app scales all the way to zero and you pay nothing for compute. A request arrives, Container Apps cold-starts a replica, and you're serving again.

There's one trap, and it's the whole reason this section exists:

<Aside type="danger" title="The database does NOT wake up on a request">
Scaling your *app* to zero is free and safe. But a request that cold-starts your app does **not** wake the database. If you also stop the database to save money, a cold-started replica boots, tries to connect, and finds nothing there — the request fails.
</Aside>

You have two workable options:

1. **Keep the database always-on (recommended).** Leave the Flexible Server running 24/7. On `B1ms` this is cheap enough that it's the right default. A cold-started app replica always finds a live database, and the only thing scaling to zero is your (free-at-idle) compute.

2. **Scheduled stop during known off-hours.** Flexible Server supports a scheduled stop/start. If a client genuinely has hours where nobody touches the system (say, overnight), you can stop the database then and accept a **dark window** — any request during the stop window fails until the database is started again. Only do this when you're certain about the traffic pattern; the savings on `B1ms` are small and the failure mode is real.

### Pair the health probes

NeoHaskell serves two HTTP endpoints out of the box — use both in your Container Apps probes:

- **`GET /health`** — *liveness.* Returns `200 {"status":"ok"}` once the HTTP server is up. Tells Container Apps the replica is alive.
- **`GET /ready`** — *readiness.* Returns `503` while the app is still rebuilding its query projections after a cold start, then `200 {"status":"ready"}` once every projection has caught up. Tells the load balancer not to send traffic until the read models are current.

```yaml
# Container Apps / Kubernetes-style probes
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
```

The readiness gate matters most on a scale-from-zero cold start against a non-empty event store: the app needs a moment to replay projections, and `/ready` holds traffic back until it's genuinely ready to answer queries correctly.

## Storage growth and cost

Flexible Server storage is **provisioned and grows-only**. You pick a size up front; you can grow it later, but you **cannot shrink it** without a dump-and-restore. An event store only ever accumulates events, so plan for steady growth.

A few cost realities to keep in mind:

- **Classic Premium SSD is tiered.** Storage comes in fixed steps — 32 GiB, 64 GiB, 128 GiB, and up — at roughly **$0.115 per GiB-month** (approximate; check the current [Azure pricing calculator](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator/), it varies by region and changes over time). **IOPS are coupled to the size** on this tier — a bigger disk buys more IOPS. If you need more throughput, you grow the disk.

- **Premium SSD v2 needs General Purpose.** The newer Premium SSD v2 (which decouples IOPS from size) is **not available on the Burstable tier** — it requires General Purpose or higher. On `B1ms` you're on classic Premium SSD.

<Aside type="caution" title="The backup-and-GRS cost trap">
Backups up to **100% of your provisioned storage** are **free**. Beyond that, backup storage is billed — and **Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS)** roughly doubles the backup footprint. The usual way to get surprised is a long **point-in-time-recovery (PITR) retention window** on a store that's growing: the retained backups quietly exceed 100% of provisioned storage and you start paying, with GRS multiplying it. **Cap your PITR retention** to what the client actually needs, and watch the backup-storage line as the event log grows.
</Aside>

## Troubleshooting

### Live projections stopped updating, but commands still work

Almost always the **direct-5432 rule**: you're connected through the PgBouncer pooler on `6432`, which silently drops `LISTEN/NOTIFY`. Set `DB_PORT=5432` and restart.

### `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`

You've hit the `B1ms` connection ceiling. Count your active stream subscriptions (each holds one connection) against [the budget](#the-connection-budget-on-b1ms). Reduce concurrent subscriptions, or move to a larger tier and raise `DB_POOL_SIZE`.

### First request after a quiet period fails to connect

Your database is stopped. With Container Apps scale-to-zero, a request wakes the *app*, not the *database*. Keep the database always-on, or confirm it isn't inside a scheduled stop window.

### TLS connection fails after turning on `verify-full`

Your CA bundle is probably wrong. Use the **root** CAs only (DigiCert Global Root G2 + Microsoft RSA Root CA 2017) — not an intermediate, which rotates. If you don't need server authentication, `DB_SSL_MODE=require` gives you downgrade protection with no certificate to manage.

## Where to go from here

- **[PostgreSQL event store](/guides/postgresql-event-store/)** — sizing, backups, replication, and the connection pool in more depth.
- **[Deployment](/guides/deployment/)** — building the container image and the rest of the deploy pipeline.
- **[Error handling](/guides/error-handling/)** — what your app does when the database blips.

Stuck for more than 15 minutes? That's on us, not you. Join our [Discord](https://discord.gg/wDj3UYzec8) — we'd love to help you get your client deployed.
