# common-errors.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/common-errors.mdx

title: "Common errors"
description: "The specific errors you will actually hit, organized by what you were doing when you hit them. Each with a direct fix."
sidebar:
  order: 4

Rather than a generic "here are the error categories" page, this is a catalog of specific errors keyed to the situation that produces them. When you see one of these, jump to the section and apply the fix.

## When adding a new event type

### "Non-exhaustive patterns in function update"

You added a new variant to an event type and didn't handle it everywhere.

**Fix:** Add a branch for the new variant in:

- The `update` function
- The `getEventEntityIdImpl` function (if the new event has an `entityId` field)
- Any `combine` function in queries that cares about the new event

The compiler will walk you through each one.

### "Non-exhaustive patterns in function getEventEntityIdImpl"

Same cause as above — same fix.

## When adding a new command

### "Could not deduce (Record.KnownSymbol ...) arising from a use of 'command'"

You forgot to provide a `NameOf` instance for your command type.

**Fix:** The `command ''Foo` macro line at the bottom of your command file generates this automatically — make sure you haven't removed it. If you still get the error after the macro line, check that the command type is at the top level of the module and is exported.

### "No instance for (Schema.ToSchema ...) arising from a use of 'command'"

Your command type needs a `ToSchema` instance so NeoHaskell can generate the OpenAPI spec.

**Fix:** Add `deriving (Generic)` to the command type and import `import Schema qualified`. The `command ''Foo` line will derive the rest.

### "No instance for (Json.FromJSON ...)"

Same fix — ensure `deriving (Generic)` and add `instance Json.FromJSON YourCommand`.

### "Couldn't match type 'EventOf EntityOf SomeCommand'"

You declared `EntityOf SomeCommand = Foo` but `Foo`'s `EventOf` isn't what `decide` returns.

**Fix:** Verify the chain:
- `EntityOf YourCommand = YourEntity`
- `EventOf YourEntity = YourEvent`
- `decide ... -> Decision YourEvent`

All three must line up. The compiler error usually names exactly which link is broken.

## When adding a new service

### "Event type mismatch in service definition!"

You tried to register two commands in the same service, but they have different event types.

**Fix:** Put each command in a service matching its entity/event type. If you have `CartCommand`s and `OrderCommand`s, you need `cartService` and `orderService` as two separate things. The compiler error names the specific command that caused the mismatch.

### "No instance for (ServiceEventType cmds)"

Your service has no commands registered yet.

**Fix:** Add at least one `|> Service.command @SomeCommand`.

## When adding a new query

### "No instance for (QueryOf Foo Bar)"

You declared a query that depends on entity `Foo` but didn't write the `QueryOf Foo Bar` instance.

**Fix:** Add:

```haskell
instance QueryOf Foo Bar where
  queryId foo = foo.id
  combine foo existing = Update Bar { ... }
```

### "deriveQuery: symbol already exists"

Two different query types were derived with the same name.

**Fix:** Rename one of them. Each query type gets a `NameOf` instance based on its type name — the kebab-case form — so `MyQuery` and `MyOtherQuery` both get unique names, but `MyQuery` in two modules collides.

## When wiring the application

### "withEventStore requires withConfig when the factory uses the config parameter"

You called `withEventStore makePostgresConfig` where `makePostgresConfig` takes your config type, but you never called `withConfig @MyConfig`.

**Fix:** Add `|> Application.withConfig @MyConfig` before the `withEventStore` call. Or, if you don't need config, use the `@()` form: `withEventStore @() (\_ -> someConfig)`.

### "No EventStore configured. Use withEventStore."

You called `Application.run` without ever calling `withEventStore`.

**Fix:** Add `|> Application.withEventStore ...` to the builder chain.

### "Application.withConfig called twice. Only one config per Application is supported."

You chained `withConfig` twice with different types.

**Fix:** Consolidate into a single config type that contains everything you need.

### "Transport not registered: &lt;name&gt;"

Your command declares a transport via `TransportsOf`, but the application hasn't registered that transport with `withTransport`.

**Fix:** Add `|> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server` (or whichever transport the command expects) to the builder chain.

## When running tests

### "cabal: No such target component: nhcore-test-core"

You're running tests from the wrong directory, or the test suite name doesn't match.

**Fix:** Run `cabal test` (no arguments) to run all suites. If you want a specific suite, check the `.cabal` file for the exact name.

### "Test suite failed to build"

Your test file has a compile error. Look at the output above the "test suite failed to build" line for the actual error.

### "Connection refused (127.0.0.1:5432)"

You're running a test suite that requires PostgreSQL, but PostgreSQL isn't running.

**Fix:** Start PostgreSQL:

```bash
docker run -d --name neohaskell-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=neohaskell \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=neohaskell \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=neohaskell \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  postgres:16-alpine
```

Or run only the suites that don't need Postgres: `cabal test nhcore-test-core`.

## When running the app

### "No EventStore configured"

You called `Application.run` without `withEventStore`.

**Fix:** Add `withEventStore` to the builder chain.

### "Connection refused" on startup

PostgreSQL isn't running, or the credentials in your config don't match.

**Fix:** Verify PostgreSQL is up and the `DB_HOST`, `DB_PORT`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_NAME` environment variables match. For local dev, the template uses `localhost`, `5432`, `neohaskell`, `neohaskell`, `neohaskell`.

### "Event store schema migration failed"

The database user doesn't have permission to create tables.

**Fix:** Grant the necessary privileges, or use a superuser account for local development.

### "Command dispatched to unknown transport"

An integration tried to dispatch a command, but the command's `TransportsOf` does not include a transport that's registered with the app.

**Fix:** Ensure the command has `InternalTransport` listed in `TransportsOf`, or register the public transport it expects.

## When deploying

### "binary not found" in production

You forgot to `cabal build` before deploying, or the deploy artifact doesn't include the binary.

**Fix:** Your deploy script should run `cabal build` inside the Nix dev shell and copy the resulting binary from `dist-newstyle/build/...` to the deploy target.

### "Glibc version mismatch"

You built the binary on one Linux version and deployed to another with an incompatible libc.

**Fix:** Build inside a container that matches your deploy environment, or use static linking via `ghc-options: -static`.

### "FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry"

PostgreSQL is rejecting the connection because of access control rules.

**Fix:** Update `pg_hba.conf` on the Postgres server to allow connections from your application host.

## General debugging habits

When you're stuck:

1. **Rebuild from scratch.** `cabal clean && cabal build` clears any stale build cache.
2. **Read the error summary, not the whole wall of text.** The first line of the error is usually the real problem; everything else is consequences.
3. **Add a type annotation.** If a type error looks confusing, add an explicit type signature to the problematic expression. Often the annotation either fixes the problem or produces a better error.
4. **Check the imports.** Many "variable not in scope" errors come from forgetting to import a module.
5. **Ask in Discord.** The [NeoHaskell Discord](https://discord.gg/wDj3UYzec8) has people who have seen every error on this page and many that aren't.

## Where to go from here

- **[Reading error messages](/guides/reading-error-messages/)** — general strategy for GHC errors.
- **[Error handling](/guides/error-handling/)** — runtime errors, not compile-time errors.
- **[Testing](/guides/testing/)** — how to catch errors before production.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.6

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/deployment.mdx

title: "Deployment"
description: "How to take a NeoHaskell application from source to running service: build pipeline, containerization, configuration, health checks, and rollbacks."
sidebar:
  order: 6

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A NeoHaskell application compiles to a single static binary. Deploying one is mechanically simple — you build, you copy, you run. This guide covers the practical concerns: how to structure your build pipeline, how to package the binary, how to manage configuration across environments, and what to watch during rollouts.

## The short version

1. Build your binary inside the Nix dev shell with `cabal build`.
2. Copy the binary to a container image or a target host.
3. Provide configuration via environment variables.
4. Run the binary as a long-running process.
5. Watch the `/health` endpoint for readiness and liveness.

That's it. Everything else is refinement.

## Build pipeline

### Building locally

Inside the Nix dev shell:

```bash
nix develop
cabal build
```

The binary ends up somewhere under `dist-newstyle/build/`. The exact path depends on your architecture and version. To find it:

```bash
cabal list-bin exe:your-app-name
```

Copy that path to a more convenient location:

```bash
cp "$(cabal list-bin exe:your-app-name)" ./dist/your-app
```

### Building in CI

The cleanest CI approach is to use `nix develop` inside your CI runner. On GitHub Actions with Determinate Nix:

```yaml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: DeterminateSystems/determinate-nix-action@v17
      - uses: cachix/cachix-action@v17
        with:
          name: neohaskell
      - run: nix develop --command cabal build
      - run: nix develop --command cabal test
      - name: Extract binary
        run: |
          mkdir -p dist
          cp "$(nix develop --command cabal list-bin exe:your-app)" dist/your-app
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: binary
          path: dist/your-app
```

The Cachix action reuses the NeoHaskell binary cache, which makes `nix develop` finish in a minute or two instead of half an hour.

### Reproducible builds with Nix

For maximum reproducibility, build via `nix build` instead of `cabal build`. This pins every dependency to exact versions from the flake lockfile. It's slower on first run but guarantees bit-for-bit reproducibility across machines.

```bash
nix build .#your-app
./result/bin/your-app --version
```

## Containerization

### The simple approach: a multi-stage Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.6

FROM nixos/nix:latest AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY . .
RUN nix --experimental-features "nix-command flakes" \
    develop --command cabal build
RUN mkdir -p /out && \
    cp "$(nix --experimental-features "nix-command flakes" \
           develop --command cabal list-bin exe:your-app)" /out/your-app

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      ca-certificates \
      libgmp10 \
      libnuma1 \
      && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY --from=builder /out/your-app /usr/local/bin/your-app
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/your-app"]
```

This produces an image around 100 MB — most of it is the debian base + a handful of shared libraries needed by the GHC runtime.

### The smaller approach: static linking

For the smallest possible image, build with static linking:

```bash
cabal build --ghc-options="-static -optl-static -optl-pthread"
```

You can then use a `scratch` or `distroless` base image:

```dockerfile
FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /out/your-app /your-app
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/your-app"]
```

Static linking has some GHC quirks (issues around `libc` and name resolution), so test carefully in your target environment before committing to it.

### The Nix-native approach

If you're comfortable with Nix, build the container image with `nix build .#container` and pull the result into your registry without ever touching Docker:

```nix
# flake.nix
outputs = { self, nixpkgs, ... }: {
  packages.x86_64-linux.container = pkgs.dockerTools.buildImage {
    name = "your-app";
    tag = "latest";
    config = {
      Cmd = [ "${self.packages.x86_64-linux.default}/bin/your-app" ];
      ExposedPorts."8080/tcp" = {};
    };
  };
};
```

This produces a minimal image with exactly the runtime dependencies your app needs. It's also fully reproducible — same inputs, same image hash.

## Running the binary

NeoHaskell applications read configuration from environment variables (via the `Config` system). You start them like any other long-running process:

```bash
DB_HOST=postgres.internal \
DB_PORT=5432 \
DB_USER=myapp \
DB_PASSWORD=$(vault read -field=password secrets/myapp/db) \
DB_NAME=myapp \
HTTP_PORT=8080 \
LOG_LEVEL=info \
./your-app
```

The app prints structured logs to stdout. In a container, these are picked up automatically by your log collector.

## Health checks

NeoHaskell exposes two endpoints by default — a **liveness** check at `/health` and a **readiness** check at `/ready`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/health
# {"status":"ok"}     — the HTTP server is up

curl http://localhost:8080/ready
# {"status":"ready"}  — every query projection has caught up
```

`/health` reports the process is alive. `/ready` returns `503` while the app is still rebuilding its query projections (for example, right after a cold start against a non-empty event store) and flips to `200` once they're current — so the load balancer holds traffic back until the read models can answer correctly.

For Kubernetes (or Azure Container Apps), point liveness at `/health` and readiness at `/ready`:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
```

The health check verifies the HTTP server is responding. If you want to include "can I reach the database?" in the check, customize it with `withHealthCheck`:

```haskell
Application.new
  |> Application.withHealthCheck @() (\_ ->
       Web.HealthCheckConfig { healthPath = "health" })
```

For more sophisticated health checks (e.g., "can I reach the database *and* the message broker"), you'd customize the path and the handler. The base health check is fine for most services.

## Configuration management

Follow the [Twelve-Factor App](https://12factor.net/config) principle: configuration lives in environment variables, not in the binary.

The `Config` system makes this ergonomic — every field you declare with `defineConfig` becomes an environment variable by default. For secrets (database passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys), use `Config.secret` and load them from a real secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secret).

For local development, the template supports `.env` files:

```env
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_USER=neohaskell
DB_PASSWORD=neohaskell
DB_NAME=neohaskell
```

`Application.run` automatically loads `.env` if present, so you can just `cabal run` and have the right config.

## Rollouts

Because NeoHaskell apps are stateless (state lives in the event store), rolling deployments work the same as any other web service.

### Blue/green or canary

1. Deploy the new version alongside the old one.
2. Route a small percentage of traffic to the new version.
3. Watch error rates, latency, and custom metrics.
4. Gradually shift traffic.
5. Retire the old version.

The event store handles schema migrations idempotently, so running two versions against the same event store at the same time is safe as long as both versions are ABI-compatible with the schema. (Usually they are; NeoHaskell never makes breaking schema changes within a minor version.)

### Zero-downtime deploys

For zero-downtime deploys, use a rolling update that takes instances out of the load balancer before terminating them. `/health` reports the app as healthy once it's finished loading; the load balancer stops sending traffic once the process is told to drain.

Integrations are a wrinkle: inbound integrations with long-running loops (like timers) should be drained gracefully before the process exits. NeoHaskell doesn't currently have a built-in "graceful shutdown" hook — you'd need to trap SIGTERM and give the integrations a few seconds to finish. This is on the roadmap.

## Observability

The minimum viable observability setup:

- **Structured logs to stdout.** NeoHaskell already does this.
- **Error alerting.** Wire your log collector to alert on any `ERROR`-level log.
- **Latency percentiles.** Measure p50, p95, p99 for each command type at the transport layer.
- **Event append rate.** Useful for capacity planning.
- **Database connection pool metrics.** Watch for exhaustion.

For Prometheus-style metrics export, NeoHaskell doesn't currently have a first-class integration — you'd add one yourself with a small custom integration. Expect this to be built-in soon.

## Rollbacks

A rollback is redeploying the previous binary. Because state is in the event store (which is backwards-compatible across versions), rolling back is safe as long as the schema hasn't changed in a breaking way.

Two things to watch:

1. **Projections rebuilt under the new version** may have a shape that old code doesn't understand. If you introduced a new field in a projection, the old code won't know about it. This is usually harmless (the field is just ignored), but verify.
2. **Events emitted under the new version** are still in the store after rollback. Make sure the old code handles them gracefully (usually by ignoring unknown variants — NeoHaskell does this via the `AnyStreamState` insertion type and the exhaustiveness checks in `update`).

## Deploying on Azure (Container Apps + Flexible Server)

The cheap, repeatable cloud setup we use for client projects is **Azure Container Apps** (scale-to-zero) in front of **Azure Database for PostgreSQL — Flexible Server** (Burstable `B1ms`). It needs no code change — just the environment variables above plus a couple of operational rules.

The one trap worth flagging here: with Container Apps `minReplicas=0`, your app scales to zero when idle, but **a request that cold-starts your app does not wake the database**. Keep the Flexible Server always-on (it's cheap on `B1ms`) so a cold-started replica always finds a live database. Pair the `/health` (liveness) and `/ready` (readiness) probes above so traffic waits for projections to catch up after a cold start.

<Aside type="caution" title="Connect on the direct port 5432, never the pooler on 6432">
Flexible Server's larger tiers ship a built-in PgBouncer pooler on `6432` whose transaction mode silently breaks `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, killing live projections and integrations with no error. Always set `DB_PORT=5432`.
</Aside>

The full runbook — connection budget, TLS hardening, scheduled-stop tradeoffs, and storage cost — is in **[Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server](/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server/)**.

## Where to go from here

- **[Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server](/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server/)** — the full golden-path runbook for the Container Apps + Flexible Server deployment.
- **[PostgreSQL event store](/guides/postgresql-event-store/)** — production persistence details.
- **[Adopting at work](/guides/adopting-at-work/)** — how to introduce NeoHaskell deployments into an existing infrastructure.
- **[Error handling](/guides/error-handling/)** — what happens when things go wrong.

# error-handling.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/error-handling.mdx

title: "Error handling"
description: "When to reject, when to throw, when to use Result, and how to keep your errors typed and recoverable."
sidebar:
  order: 2

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

NeoHaskell gives you three ways to represent something going wrong: `Decider.reject`, `Task.throw`, and `Result`. They're not interchangeable. Picking the right one matters for both correctness and operational clarity.

This guide explains when to use each, how they compose, and the specific patterns you'll see in real code.

## The three error types

| Mechanism | Lives in | Used for | Carries |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`Decider.reject reason`** | `Decision` (pure) | Business rule violations inside a command | A `Text` reason |
| **`Task.throw err`** | `Task err val` (effectful) | System failures — I/O, network, etc. | A typed error of your choice |
| **`Result err val`** | Any (pure) | Pure computations that can fail | A typed error |

## When to use `Decider.reject`

Use rejection for **expected business outcomes** inside a command's `decide` function.

- "Account doesn't exist."
- "Insufficient balance."
- "Email already registered."
- "Permission denied."

A rejection is not a bug. It's a normal, expected outcome — the domain told the caller no. The caller gets a structured `Rejected` response with the reason; your logs stay quiet.

```haskell
decide :: Deposit -> Maybe Account -> RequestContext -> Decision AccountEvent
decide cmd account _ctx = case account of
  Nothing -> Decider.reject "Account does not exist"
  Just _  -> if cmd.amount <= 0
    then Decider.reject "Amount must be positive"
    else Decider.acceptExisting [ MoneyDeposited { ... } ]
```

Rejection reasons are free text. Keep them user-friendly — they might appear in an API response, an error toast, or a metric label. Use full sentences, not codes.

<Aside type="note" title="Why not use exceptions?">
If you threw an exception from `decide`, the command executor would catch it as an unexpected failure and log it as an error. That's wrong — the command simply wasn't accepted. Rejection is the semantic fit.
</Aside>

## When to use `Task.throw`

Use `Task.throw` for **unexpected system failures** in effectful code (anywhere you're inside a `Task`).

- "Database connection lost."
- "External API returned 503."
- "Failed to parse configuration file."
- "Deserialization failed."

`Task.throw` puts a typed error into the failure channel of the `Task`. It propagates up through `<-` bindings until someone catches it with `Task.recover` or until it reaches the top of the call stack.

```haskell
fetchConfig :: Path -> Task Text Config
fetchConfig path = do
  contents <- readFile path
  case parseConfig contents of
    Ok config -> Task.yield config
    Err parseError -> Task.throw [fmt|Invalid config at #{path}: #{parseError}|]
```

Notice that the error channel is `Text` here — a human-readable message. For richer errors, use a sum type:

```haskell
data ConfigError
  = FileNotFound Path
  | ParseError Text
  | MissingRequiredField Text

fetchConfig :: Path -> Task ConfigError Config
fetchConfig path = do
  contents <- readFile path |> Task.mapError (\_ -> FileNotFound path)
  case parseConfig contents of
    Ok config -> Task.yield config
    Err parseError -> Task.throw (ParseError parseError)
```

Typed errors let callers switch on the failure type and react differently to different causes.

## When to use `Result`

Use `Result err val` in **pure code** that can fail but isn't inside a `Task`.

```haskell
parseAge :: Text -> Result Text Int
parseAge text = case Int.fromText text of
  Nothing -> Err "not a valid integer"
  Just n -> if n < 0 then Err "age must be non-negative" else Ok n
```

`Result` is the pure cousin of `Task`. It's what you use inside `decide` functions (which are pure), or in helper functions that don't need side effects.

Converting a `Result` to a `Task`:

```haskell
fromResult :: Result err val -> Task err val
fromResult r = case r of
  Ok v -> Task.yield v
  Err e -> Task.throw e
```

## The decision tree

Use this to pick the right tool:

```
Is the failure a business rule violation inside a decide function?
├── YES → Decider.reject
└── NO  → Is the code inside a Task?
         ├── YES → Task.throw
         └── NO  → Result
```

## Propagation

Errors propagate automatically in `do` blocks. If any `<-` step fails, the rest of the block is skipped:

```haskell
loadDashboard :: Uuid -> Task Text Dashboard
loadDashboard userId = do
  user <- fetchUser userId       -- if this fails, posts/stats are never fetched
  posts <- fetchPosts userId     -- if this fails, stats is never fetched
  stats <- fetchStats userId
  Task.yield Dashboard { user = user, posts = posts, stats = stats }
```

If `fetchUser` fails, the whole task fails with whatever error `fetchUser` threw. The caller sees the error; you didn't have to write try/catch.

## Recovering from errors

Three ways to recover:

### `Task.recover`

Run a recovery function when the task fails:

```haskell
fetchUserOrDefault :: Uuid -> Task err User
fetchUserOrDefault userId =
  fetchUser userId
    |> Task.recover (\_err -> Task.yield defaultUser)
```

### `Task.asResult`

Convert a failing task into one that always succeeds with a `Result`:

```haskell
handleRequest :: Uuid -> Task err Text
handleRequest userId = do
  result <- Task.asResult (fetchUser userId)
  case result of
    Ok user -> Task.yield [fmt|Hello, #{user.name}|]
    Err reason -> Task.yield [fmt|Could not load user: #{reason}|]
```

### `Task.mapError`

Transform one error type into another as the task propagates:

```haskell
readConfigTyped :: Path -> Task AppError Config
readConfigTyped path =
  readConfig path
    |> Task.mapError (\textErr -> AppConfigError textErr)
```

This is how you compose errors across layers: the lower layer uses its own error type, the upper layer converts as it wraps.

## Composing errors across services

Different parts of your system may use different error types. The pattern is:

1. **Each service layer uses its native error type.** The event store uses `EventStoreError`. The HTTP transport uses `Text`. Your integration uses `IntegrationError`. Etc.
2. **Adapters map between layers.** When you call the event store from an integration, you `Task.mapError` to convert.
3. **At the top of the call stack, you have one type.** Usually `Text`, often wrapped in a richer type that includes the layer the error came from.

A typical wrapper:

```haskell
data AppError
  = EventStoreFailure Text
  | IntegrationFailure IntegrationError
  | ValidationFailure Text

runApp :: Application -> Task AppError Unit
runApp app = do
  Application.run app |> Task.mapError EventStoreFailure
```

## Logging errors

When you catch an error, log it before recovering:

```haskell
fetchWithFallback :: Uuid -> Task err User
fetchWithFallback userId =
  fetchUser userId
    |> Task.recover (\err -> do
        Log.warn [fmt|fetchUser failed for #{userId}: #{err}. Using fallback.|]
        Task.ignoreError
        fetchUserFromReplica userId)
```

A rule of thumb: **every caught error should be logged somewhere**. Silently swallowed errors are the source of half of all production mysteries.

## Rejection reasons vs. error messages

Rejection reasons (from `Decider.reject`) are **user-facing**. They should be actionable by the caller:

- ✅ "Insufficient funds"
- ✅ "Email must be a valid address"
- ✅ "This account is closed and cannot accept deposits"
- ❌ "Balance check failed at line 47 of Withdraw.hs"
- ❌ "null pointer at AccountService.java:213"

Error messages (from `Task.throw`) are **developer-facing**. They go to logs and alerting, not to users:

- ✅ "Failed to connect to PostgreSQL: connection refused (127.0.0.1:5432)"
- ✅ "JSON decode failed at offset 142: expected integer, got string"
- ✅ "OAuth2 token refresh failed: invalid_grant"

Never show a raw `Task.throw` error to an end user. Wrap it and replace the message with something helpful.

## Pattern: authorization inside decide

A common pattern you'll see in real codebases:

```haskell
decide cmd entity ctx = case ctx.user of
  Nothing ->
    Decider.reject "Authentication required"
  Just user ->
    case entity of
      Nothing ->
        Decider.reject "Resource does not exist"
      Just e ->
        if e.ownerId /= user.sub
          then Decider.reject "You do not own this resource"
          else -- ... proceed
            Decider.acceptExisting [ ... ]
```

Authorization failures are rejections, not exceptions. They're expected outcomes — the caller asked for something they're not allowed to do. Log them if you want (for audit), but don't treat them as bugs.

## Pattern: graceful degradation

When a secondary feature fails, let the primary feature succeed:

```haskell
serveHomepage :: Task err HomepageHtml
serveHomepage = do
  posts <- fetchPosts  -- primary data
  sidebar <- fetchSidebar
    |> Task.recover (\_err -> Task.yield emptySidebar)  -- graceful fallback
  Task.yield (render posts sidebar)
```

If the sidebar service is down, the user still sees the posts. If the main data fails, the whole request fails.

## Pattern: retry with backoff

For transient failures, retry with exponential backoff:

```haskell
import Timer qualified

retryWithBackoff :: Int -> Task err val -> Task err val
retryWithBackoff maxAttempts action = go 1
  where
    go attempt
      | attempt >= maxAttempts = action
      | otherwise =
          action |> Task.recover (\_err -> do
            Timer.sleep (Timer.seconds (2 ^ attempt))
            go (attempt + 1))
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Let the executor handle command retries">
The command executor already retries on concurrency conflicts automatically. Don't wrap commands in your own retry logic — you'll double up.
</Aside>

## Where to go from here

- **[Effects and concurrency](/concepts/effects/)** — deeper look at `Task`.
- **[Reading error messages](/guides/reading-error-messages/)** — specifically for compiler errors.
- **[Testing](/guides/testing/)** — how to test error paths.

# integrating-existing-systems.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/integrating-existing-systems.mdx

title: "Integrating existing systems"
description: "Inbound and outbound integrations, webhook handlers, and connecting NeoHaskell to services you already run."
sidebar:
  order: 7

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The world does not consist of NeoHaskell applications. Your system needs to talk to existing databases, third-party APIs, message brokers, payment processors, email services, and the occasional shell script. This guide shows the patterns.

NeoHaskell calls external connections **integrations**. There are two kinds:

- **Outbound integrations** react to domain events by doing things in the outside world (or emitting follow-up commands). Examples: send an email when a user registers, call a payment processor when an order is placed, publish to Kafka when an invoice is paid.
- **Inbound integrations** take input from the outside world (webhooks, polling, timers) and convert it into commands. Examples: accept Stripe webhooks and emit `PaymentReceived` commands, poll an SFTP drop every hour and emit `FileDelivered` commands, fire a `DailyReport` command on a schedule.

Both are first-class, typed, and compile-checked. You don't use a message queue client; you don't write a webhook controller; you don't set up a cron job. You write an integration and plug it into the application.

## Outbound integrations

An outbound integration listens for events on a specific entity type and produces actions in response. The shape is:

```haskell
instance OutboundIntegration MyIntegration where
  reactTo _config entity event = case event of
    SomeEvent { ... } -> Integration.batch [ ... actions ... ]
    _ -> Integration.none
```

`reactTo` is a pure function. It takes the current entity state, the new event, and returns a collection of actions to execute. Actions might be:

- Emitting a follow-up command (`Integration.emitCommand`).
- Making an HTTP call (via a custom `Action` implementation).
- Writing to a shared database.
- Enqueueing a job in a traditional queue.

### Example: email on signup

Let's build an integration that sends a welcome email when a user registers. We'll assume you have a `Sendgrid` module somewhere that knows how to POST to Sendgrid's API.

```haskell
module MyApp.User.Integrations.WelcomeEmail (
  WelcomeEmail (..),
) where

import Core
import Integration qualified
import MyApp.User.Core (User, UserEvent (..))
import Service.OutboundIntegration.Core (OutboundIntegration (..))
import Sendgrid qualified

data WelcomeEmail = WelcomeEmail

type instance EntityOf WelcomeEmail = User

instance OutboundIntegration WelcomeEmail where
  reactTo _config user event = case event of
    UserRegistered { email } ->
      Integration.batch
        [ Integration.outbound
            Sendgrid.Email
              { to = email
              , templateId = "welcome-template"
              , variables = Map.fromList [("name", user.name)]
              }
        ]

    _ -> Integration.none
```

The `Sendgrid.Email` record is a **config record** — it describes what email to send. `Sendgrid` provides a `ToAction` instance that turns the config into an actual HTTP call. You don't write HTTP-handling code inside the integration; you describe what you want, and the library knows how to do it.

Register the integration with the application:

```haskell
app :: Application
app = Application.new
  |> Application.withEventStore ...
  |> Application.withService userService
  |> Application.withOutbound @WelcomeEmail
```

Done. Every `UserRegistered` event now fires a welcome email, with retry logic and error handling managed by the runtime.

### Example: forwarding to Kafka

If you have a Kafka-based event backbone and want NeoHaskell events to flow into it, you build an outbound integration that publishes to Kafka:

```haskell
instance OutboundIntegration KafkaForwarder where
  reactTo _config _entity event =
    Integration.batch
      [ Integration.outbound
          Kafka.Publish
            { topic = "user-events"
            , key = Json.encodeText event
            , payload = Json.encodeText event
            }
      ]
```

Now every event on the `User` entity is mirrored to Kafka. Downstream services (Spark jobs, analytics, legacy systems) can subscribe to the Kafka topic without knowing anything about NeoHaskell.

### Example: emitting a follow-up command

Integrations can also emit commands back into the system — this is how sagas work. When event A happens, run command B:

```haskell
instance OutboundIntegration OrderToInventory where
  reactTo _config _order event = case event of
    OrderPlaced { items, orderId } ->
      Integration.batch
        [ Integration.outbound
            ReserveItems
              { orderId = orderId
              , items = items
              }
        ]

    _ -> Integration.none
```

`ReserveItems` is a command on the inventory service (marked `InternalTransport` so it's not exposed via HTTP). The integration emits it; the runtime dispatches it to the inventory service. The two services remain decoupled — neither calls the other directly.

## Outbound integrations with lifecycle

Some integrations have state that spans multiple events. For example, a rate limiter that tracks API calls per user, or a batch emitter that buffers events and flushes periodically. For these, use `withOutboundLifecycle`:

```haskell
-- A stateful integration that batches events
batchingIntegration :: OutboundLifecycleIntegration User UserEvent
batchingIntegration = do
  buffer <- ConcurrentVar.new Array.empty
  -- ... construct the integration with access to `buffer` ...
```

Lifecycle integrations are more advanced; see the testbed for a full example.

## Inbound integrations

Inbound integrations take input from the outside world and feed it into NeoHaskell as commands.

### Example: a periodic timer

```haskell
import Integration.Timer qualified as Timer
import MyApp.Report.Commands.GenerateDailyReport (GenerateDailyReport (..))

dailyReportTimer :: Integration.Inbound
dailyReportTimer =
  Timer.every
    Timer.Every
      { interval = Timer.hours 24
      , toCommand = \_ -> GenerateDailyReport {}
      }
```

Every 24 hours, this fires a `GenerateDailyReport` command. The command is dispatched through the same command executor as external commands — so it goes through `decide`, produces events, updates projections, etc. The timer is just an event producer.

Register it:

```haskell
Application.new
  |> ...
  |> Application.withInbound @() (\_ -> dailyReportTimer)
```

### Example: a webhook handler

For webhooks from services like Stripe or Slack, the pattern is:

1. Add a public HTTP route that accepts the webhook payload.
2. Validate the webhook signature.
3. Convert the payload to a command.
4. Dispatch the command.

You can do this inside a custom inbound integration:

```haskell
stripeWebhook :: Integration.Inbound
stripeWebhook = Integration.inbound
  InboundConfig
    { run = \emit -> do
        Http.serve "/webhooks/stripe" \request -> do
          verified <- Stripe.verifySignature request
          case verified of
            Ok event ->
              emit (PaymentReceived { paymentId = event.id, ... })
            Err reason -> do
              Log.warn [fmt|Invalid Stripe signature: #{reason}|]
              Task.yield ()
    }
```

The `emit` callback dispatches the command into the NeoHaskell system.

## Integrations are typed

Every integration has a specific entity type and event type it reacts to. The compiler enforces that:

- The event type matches the entity's event type.
- Commands you emit are registered with the application.
- The transports required by emitted commands are registered.

This is a big deal in practice. In a Kafka-based system, you might have a producer publishing "UserCreated" and a consumer listening for "UserCreated" — but if someone renames the event, the two are silently desynced until a test fails. In NeoHaskell, the sync is a type constraint; the compiler rejects the rename unless both sides are updated.

## Handling failure in integrations

Integrations can fail. An HTTP call might return 503. An email service might be rate-limited. A downstream command might be rejected.

The integration runtime handles transient failures with retries (with exponential backoff). For permanent failures, you handle them inside the integration's `reactTo`:

```haskell
instance OutboundIntegration EmailOrLog where
  reactTo _config user event = case event of
    UserRegistered { email } ->
      Integration.batch
        [ Integration.outbound (Sendgrid.Email { to = email, ... })
            -- If this fails, we also log
        , Integration.outbound
            (LogWarning { message = [fmt|Welcome email pending for #{email}|] })
        ]
    _ -> Integration.none
```

The two actions run in order. If the first fails, the second still runs (unless you explicitly decide otherwise in the action's implementation).

For persistent coordination — "if this fails, retry in 5 minutes" — you use an integration with lifecycle state, or you emit a `RetryLater` command that schedules the retry.

## Integrating with a legacy database

Sometimes you need to read from or write to a database that an old system owns. The cleanest pattern:

1. **Don't write to it from NeoHaskell directly.** Instead, emit a domain event and have an outbound integration call the legacy system's API (even if the "API" is just a SQL stored procedure).
2. **Read from it via a custom data source**, wrapped as an integration. This keeps the database access out of the domain logic.

If you truly must share a database between NeoHaskell and a legacy system, the usual pattern is to use the event store as the source of truth and expose a read replica of projections into the legacy system's schema via a separate integration.

## Integrating with message brokers

If you already use RabbitMQ, NATS, or Kafka:

- **Outbound:** Write an outbound integration that publishes events to the broker.
- **Inbound:** Write an inbound integration that subscribes to topics and emits commands.

Both are a few dozen lines of code. The hardest part is usually handling broker-specific features like consumer groups, offsets, or dead-letter queues — and those are features of the broker, not NeoHaskell.

## Strangler fig pattern

Introducing NeoHaskell into an existing system is usually a strangler fig: the old system keeps running, NeoHaskell takes over one feature at a time.

1. **Pick a bounded feature** — ideally one with a clear input/output boundary.
2. **Write the NeoHaskell service** for that feature.
3. **Route traffic through NeoHaskell** for the new feature.
4. **Use integrations** to keep old and new systems in sync where they overlap.
5. **Expand** as confidence grows.

The typical failure mode is trying to migrate everything at once. Don't. Start with one service, prove the value, expand.

## Where to go from here

- **[Adopting at work](/guides/adopting-at-work/)** — the political and organizational side.
- **[Tutorial Part 5](/tutorial/05-transfers/)** — the full worked example of cross-entity coordination via integrations.
- **[Core concepts → Services](/concepts/services/)** — why services are the right unit for integrations.

# postgresql-event-store.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/postgresql-event-store.mdx

title: "PostgreSQL event store"
description: "Running NeoHaskell with PostgreSQL in production — configuration, sizing, backup, replication, and operational concerns."
sidebar:
  order: 5

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The in-memory event store is perfect for development and tests but loses everything on restart. For production, you use PostgreSQL. This guide covers how to set it up, how to size it, how to back it up, and what to watch in production.

## Why PostgreSQL

NeoHaskell's event store is PostgreSQL-backed by design. The reasoning:

- **PostgreSQL is everywhere.** Your ops team already knows it.
- **ACID at the stream level.** Optimistic concurrency on append is atomic.
- **Great tooling.** Backup, replication, monitoring, disaster recovery — all well-established.
- **Scales further than you think.** With proper schema design and partitioning, a single Postgres instance handles tens of thousands of events per second.
- **Flexible.** If you outgrow Postgres, the event store interface is pluggable — you can swap in a custom backend.

## Switching from InMemory to Postgres

You already saw this in [Tutorial Part 6](/tutorial/06-audit-everything/). The switch is a one-line change:

```haskell
-- Before
Application.withEventStore @() (\_ -> InMemory.new)

-- After
Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig

makePostgresConfig :: NeoBankConfig -> PostgresEventStore
makePostgresConfig config =
  PostgresEventStore
    { user = config.dbUser
    , password = config.dbPassword
    , host = config.dbHost
    , databaseName = config.dbName
    , port = config.dbPort
    }
```

On startup, the event store:

1. Connects to PostgreSQL.
2. Checks that the expected schema exists, creating it if not.
3. Starts serving reads and writes.

The schema it creates is a few tables — one for events, one for stream metadata, a couple for snapshots. You don't manage them by hand; the store manages its own schema.

## Configuration

Use the `Config` system to pull credentials from environment variables:

```haskell
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}

module MyApp.Config (NeoBankConfig (..), HasNeoBankConfig) where

import Config (defineConfig)
import Config qualified
import Core

defineConfig
  "NeoBankConfig"
  [ Config.field @Text "dbHost"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL host"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("localhost" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_HOST"
  , Config.field @Int "dbPort"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL port"
      |> Config.defaultsTo (5432 :: Int)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_PORT"
  , Config.field @Text "dbUser"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL username"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("neohaskell" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_USER"
  , Config.field @Text "dbPassword"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL password"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("neohaskell" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_PASSWORD"
      |> Config.secret
  , Config.field @Text "dbName"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL database name"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("neohaskell" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_NAME"
  ]
```

`Config.secret` flags the password as sensitive, which means it won't be printed by `--help` or included in config dumps.

In production, pass the credentials via environment variables:

```bash
DB_HOST=postgres.prod.internal \
DB_PORT=5432 \
DB_USER=neobank_app \
DB_PASSWORD=$(vault read -field=password kv/neobank/db) \
DB_NAME=neobank \
./neobank
```

## Sizing a production instance

Rules of thumb for a single PostgreSQL instance:

| Load | Instance size | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| < 1k events/sec | db.t3.medium equivalent, 100 GB SSD | Comfortable headroom |
| 1k–5k events/sec | db.m6i.large / 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM | Watch WAL generation |
| 5k–20k events/sec | db.m6i.2xlarge / 8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM | Dedicate IOPS |
| 20k+ events/sec | Tune carefully; consider partitioning | Usually need custom setup |

The bottlenecks you'll hit, in order:

1. **Write IOPS.** Events are small but append-heavy. Provision enough IOPS for your peak write rate.
2. **WAL bandwidth.** Every append writes to WAL. Replication lag becomes noticeable before throughput does.
3. **Memory for indexes.** Queries against the event store need the main index in RAM for good performance.

For most applications, you never hit these limits. A comfortable default for a production system with moderate traffic is a 4 vCPU / 16 GB RAM instance with 500 GB of SSD. You can monitor and scale up from there.

## Connection pooling

NeoHaskell uses `hasql-pool` internally, with **three** pools per app, each at an explicit, deploy-tier-safe default:

| Pool | Default size | What flows through it |
|---|---|---|
| EventStore | `6` | Command appends, entity fetches, query catch-up reads |
| QueryObjectStore | `4` | Read-model writes during rebuild, read-model reads |
| FileUpload | `6` | File metadata writes (shares the EventStore pool size) |

On top of the pools, the app keeps a persistent `LISTEN/NOTIFY` listener pair (2 connections) and opens **one connection per active stream subscription**. So the steady-state demand is `6 + 4 + 6 + 2 + 1 (init) = 19` connections, plus one for each active stream subscription.

The EventStore pool size is tunable from the environment with `DB_POOL_SIZE` (default `6`), which also sizes the FileUpload pool since it shares that config. Raise it on a larger Postgres tier; the EventStore pool is the one to grow first.

```haskell
PostgresEventStore
  { ... connection fields ...
  , poolSize = 12  -- omit to use the B1ms-safe default of 6
  }
```

Postgres itself has a `max_connections` setting. Make sure it's higher than the sum of every pool plus the listener pair, per-stream subscriptions, and headroom for admin connections and background workers. On a small tier this budget is tight — see the [Flexible Server connection budget](/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server/#the-connection-budget-on-b1ms) for the full arithmetic on Azure `B1ms`.

## Running on Azure Flexible Server

If your managed Postgres is **Azure Database for PostgreSQL — Flexible Server** (our standard cloud target), two rules carry the deployment:

- **Connect on the direct port `5432`, never the PgBouncer pooler on `6432`.** PgBouncer's transaction mode silently breaks `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, so live projections and integrations stop firing with no error. On the Burstable `B1ms` tier there's no pooler, so `5432` is automatic; on larger tiers, keep `DB_PORT=5432`.
- **Optionally harden TLS** with `DB_SSL_MODE=require` (forbid silent plaintext downgrade) or `verify-full` with a root-CA bundle (`DB_SSL_ROOT_CERT`). It's off by default, so localhost and dev are unaffected, and it applies uniformly to all three pools and the `LISTEN/NOTIFY` connections.

The full golden path — connection budget, scale-to-zero pairing with Container Apps, and storage cost — lives in the dedicated **[Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server](/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server/)** guide.

## Backup and recovery

The event log is the source of truth. If you lose it, you lose your application's memory. Treat backups accordingly.

### Continuous backup (recommended)

Use PostgreSQL's continuous archiving (PITR) so you can restore to any point in time. On AWS RDS, this is "automated backups with point-in-time recovery." On self-hosted Postgres, use `pg_basebackup` + WAL archiving to S3 (or equivalent).

### Nightly snapshots

In addition to continuous backup, take a full snapshot every night and store it in a separate region. A ransomware attack or a bad migration can wipe continuous backups if they live next to the live database.

### Verify restores

A backup you haven't tested restoring is not a backup. Once a month, restore your latest backup to a scratch environment and verify that NeoHaskell can start and serve queries against it. Automate this if possible.

## Read replicas

For read-heavy workloads, you can run PostgreSQL read replicas and point your projection rebuild or query subscriber at them. This keeps the primary free for event appends.

<Aside type="caution" title="Replicas have lag">
Read replicas are eventually consistent with the primary. If your projections read from a replica, they can fall behind. This is usually fine — the projections themselves are eventually consistent with events — but make sure your SLOs account for the added lag.
</Aside>

## Partitioning

If your event volume grows large enough that a single `events` table becomes a problem (typically > 100 million rows), you can partition the table by stream or by date. PostgreSQL native partitioning works well for this.

The NeoHaskell event store does not partition automatically — you'd do this as a custom operational step. The internal layout of the events table is documented; reach out on Discord if you need help setting this up.

## Monitoring

Watch these metrics on your production event store:

- **Append latency** — p50, p95, p99. Watch for regressions.
- **Events per second** — to catch traffic spikes before they hit capacity.
- **WAL generation rate** — helps you plan replication bandwidth.
- **Connection pool utilization** — if you see 100% utilization, bump the pool size or investigate slow queries.
- **Replication lag** (if using replicas) — keep under 1s for read-your-writes safety.
- **Disk usage** — events accumulate. Plan for growth.
- **Cache hit ratio** — PostgreSQL's internal stats. A healthy database has > 99% cache hit on indexes.

NeoHaskell exposes structured logs for each command. Feed them into your observability stack (DataDog, Honeycomb, Loki, whatever) and set alerts on error rate, p99 latency, and append failures.

## Schema evolution at the database level

The event store manages its own schema. Upgrades to NeoHaskell may include schema migrations — they run on startup and are idempotent. In a zero-downtime deployment, you'd:

1. Deploy the new version to a canary instance and let it run the migration.
2. Verify the migration succeeded.
3. Roll the rest of the fleet once the schema is confirmed good.

Migrations in the NeoHaskell event store are designed to be backwards-compatible: a new version reads old events correctly without needing to rewrite them.

## Common production issues

### High WAL generation

**Symptom:** Replication is lagging or backup storage is growing fast.

**Cause:** Either many commands are being processed (legitimate) or something is causing spurious writes (bug).

**Fix:** Check command rates via your observability stack. If writes are legitimate, you may need a bigger instance or faster disks. If they're not, investigate what's generating the writes.

### Slow entity reconstruction

**Symptom:** Commands that target a single entity take longer than expected.

**Cause:** Long event streams with no recent snapshot cache. Every command reconstructs the entity from the full stream.

**Fix:** NeoHaskell takes snapshots automatically. If reconstruction is still slow, check that snapshot caching is enabled in your config and that the snapshot cache is not full.

### Connection pool exhausted

**Symptom:** Latency spikes; logs show "failed to acquire connection."

**Cause:** Too many concurrent commands for your pool size.

**Fix:** Increase pool size, ensure `max_connections` on Postgres is higher than the sum of all pool sizes, investigate whether commands are blocking longer than expected.

### Replica lag growing

**Symptom:** Projections reading from a read replica are out of date.

**Cause:** Replica hardware is slower than primary, or network bandwidth to replica is saturated.

**Fix:** Point projections at the primary temporarily, fix the replica, then switch back.

## Where to go from here

- **[Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server](/guides/azure-postgresql-flexible-server/)** — the cheap, repeatable cloud deployment on Azure `B1ms`.
- **[Deployment](/guides/deployment/)** — how to ship the compiled NeoHaskell binary.
- **[Tutorial Part 6](/tutorial/06-audit-everything/)** — the first time you switch from in-memory to Postgres.
- **[Testing](/guides/testing/)** — how to test against the real event store.

# reading-error-messages.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/guides/reading-error-messages.mdx

title: "Reading error messages"
description: "How to read NeoHaskell compiler errors — on your own, with an AI assistant, or both. The better you read them, the better you can guide your assistant."
sidebar:
  order: 3

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

NeoHaskell compiler errors are specific, actionable, and well-structured. They are also one of the best tools you have for collaborating with an AI assistant. If your assistant generates code that doesn't compile, the error is the fastest path to a fix — and understanding the error yourself is how you guide the assistant toward better output over time.

This page teaches you to read errors two ways:

1. **Reading them yourself** — for when you want to fix the problem directly.
2. **Reading them with an assistant** — for when you want to paste the error and get a fix, but you also want to understand *why* the fix works so you can steer next time.

## Why learning to read errors matters (even with AI)

You might be thinking: "I'll just paste the error into my assistant and let it fix things." That works. NeoHaskell errors are specific enough that an assistant usually fixes them in one round.

But here's the thing: **the better you understand errors, the better your prompts become.** An engineer who sees "Non-exhaustive patterns in function update" and knows it means "I added an event and forgot to handle it" will write prompts like "add a `TransferCompleted` event and make sure `update` handles it." An engineer who doesn't understand the error will write "fix whatever is wrong." The first prompt produces correct code. The second produces a guess.

Understanding errors is not about replacing your assistant. It is about becoming a better driver of it.

## The anatomy of an error

Every NeoHaskell compiler error follows the same shape:

```text
src/MyApp/Foo.hs:42:15: error:
    <summary — one or two lines>

    <detail — the specific types and what's wrong>

    |
 42 |   result = someFunction wrongArg
    |                         ^^^^^^^^
```

Four parts:

1. **Location** (`file:line:col`) — where the problem is.
2. **Summary** — what went wrong, in one sentence.
3. **Detail** — the specific types or constraints that failed.
4. **Source pointer** — the exact expression, underlined.

**Read the summary first.** It tells you the category. The detail tells you the specifics. The source pointer shows you the exact spot. Most errors can be understood from the summary alone.

### When pasting to an assistant

Paste the **entire error**, not just the summary. The assistant needs the types and the source location to give a precise fix. But read the summary yourself first — even a two-second glance builds your instinct for what went wrong, and over time you'll find yourself fixing errors faster than the assistant round-trips.

## Error catalog

Here are the errors you will actually see, what they mean, and what to tell your assistant if you want it to fix them for you.

### "Couldn't match expected type ... with actual type ..."

The most common error. A type mismatch at a specific call site.

```text
src/MyApp/Deposit.hs:15:20: error:
    • Couldn't match expected type 'Int' with actual type 'Text'
    • In the second argument of 'Deposit', namely 'amount'
      In the expression: Deposit { accountId = ..., amount = "50" }
```

**What it means:** `Deposit.amount` expects `Int`, but you passed `"50"` (a `Text`).

**How to fix it yourself:** Write `50` (without quotes), or convert with `Int.fromText "50"`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "The `amount` field is `Int` but you passed a string. Use the integer literal, not a quoted string."

### "Non-exhaustive patterns in function ..."

You added a new event variant but didn't handle it everywhere.

```text
src/MyApp/Account.hs:88:1: warning:
    Non-exhaustive patterns in function update

    In an equation for 'update':
        Patterns of type 'AccountEvent' not matched:
            MoneyWithdrawn{}
```

**What it means:** The `update` function handles some `AccountEvent` cases but not `MoneyWithdrawn`.

**How to fix it yourself:** Add a `MoneyWithdrawn` branch to the `case` expression in `update`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "You added `MoneyWithdrawn` to the event type but didn't add a case for it in the `update` function. Add a branch that handles `MoneyWithdrawn` — it should subtract the amount from the balance."

<Aside type="tip" title="This is the most important error in NeoHaskell">
This error is the compiler telling you: "you changed the domain and forgot to update the code that processes it." In other languages this is a production bug. In NeoHaskell it is a build failure. If your assistant ever generates code that adds an event without handling it, this error catches it instantly — paste it back and the assistant will add the missing branch.
</Aside>

### "Variable not in scope: ..."

A name was used but not imported.

```text
src/MyApp/Deposit.hs:12:10: error:
    Variable not in scope: Text.trim
```

**What it means:** You called `Text.trim` but didn't import the `Text` module.

**How to fix it yourself:** Add `import Text qualified` to the top of the file.

**What to tell your assistant:** "You used `Text.trim` but forgot to add `import Text qualified` at the top."

<Aside type="note" title="AI assistants drift on imports">
This is one of the most common AI mistakes — using a function from a module that isn't imported. If you see "Variable not in scope" in assistant-generated code, the fix is always the same: add the import. Over time you'll learn which modules your project uses most and can preemptively tell the assistant "make sure to import `Text qualified` and `Array qualified`."
</Aside>

### "No instance for (Entity Foo)"

You tried to use a type as an entity but didn't give it the required typeclass instance.

```text
src/MyApp/Account.hs:14:1: error:
    • No instance for (Entity Account) arising from a use of 'withService'
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Add `instance Entity Account where ...` to your `Core.hs`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "The `Account` type is missing its `Entity` instance. Add `instance Entity Account where initialStateImpl = initialState; updateImpl = update` to the Core module."

### "Event type mismatch in service definition!"

Two commands in the same service use different event types.

```text
error:
    Event type mismatch in service definition!

    All commands in a service must use the same event type.

    Expected event type: CartEvent
    But command 'ProcessPayment' uses event type: PaymentEvent

    To fix: Ensure all commands in this service share a common event type.
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Move `ProcessPayment` to its own service, or merge the event types.

**What to tell your assistant:** "The service mixes `CartEvent` and `PaymentEvent`. Move `ProcessPayment` into a separate `PaymentService` module with its own `Service.new |> Service.command @ProcessPayment`."

<Aside type="note" title="This error has a plain-English fix instruction">
NeoHaskell custom errors include a "To fix:" line. When you see one, you can paste it directly to your assistant — it is already phrased as an instruction.
</Aside>

### "Couldn't match expected type 'Task Text ...' with actual type ..."

You returned a raw value where a `Task` was expected.

```text
error:
    • Couldn't match expected type 'Task Text User'
                  with actual type 'User'
    • In the expression: someUser
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Wrap the value in `Task.yield`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "You returned a raw `User` where a `Task Text User` was expected. Wrap it in `Task.yield`."

### "Variable not in scope: pure"

You (or your assistant) used `pure` instead of `Task.yield`.

```text
error:
    Variable not in scope: pure :: User -> Task err User
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Replace `pure` with `Task.yield`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "NeoHaskell uses `Task.yield` instead of `pure`. Replace every `pure` with `Task.yield`." (This is a common AI drift — the system prompt covers it, but assistants forget.)

### "Ambiguous type variable"

The compiler can't figure out which type you meant.

```text
error:
    • Ambiguous type variable 'a0' arising from a use of 'Json.decode'
    • In the expression: Json.decode someBytes
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Add a type annotation:

```haskell
result = Json.decode @User someBytes
```

**What to tell your assistant:** "Add `@User` (or whatever the target type is) after `Json.decode` to resolve the ambiguity."

### "Orphan instance"

You defined a typeclass instance in a module that doesn't own either the typeclass or the type.

```text
warning:
    Orphan instance: instance Json.ToJSON MyType
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Move the instance to the module that defines `MyType`.

**What to tell your assistant:** "Move the `Json.ToJSON MyType` instance into the same module where `MyType` is defined."

### "Record update has multiple constructors"

You tried to update a field on a record, but the type has multiple constructors and not all of them have that field.

```text
error:
    • Record update has multiple constructors
```

**How to fix it yourself:** Use a `case` expression to handle each constructor explicitly.

**What to tell your assistant:** "The record update is ambiguous because the type has multiple constructors. Use `case event of` and handle each constructor with its own record update."

### "Could not find module 'Core'"

Your `.cabal` file isn't set up to include the NeoHaskell core library.

**How to fix it yourself:** Check that `build-depends:` includes `nhcore`. The template already does this.

**What to tell your assistant:** "The `Core` module isn't found. Check that `nhcore` is listed in `build-depends` in the `.cabal` file."

## The wall-of-text strategy

Sometimes you get a multi-screen error. Here is how to handle it, whether you're fixing it yourself or pasting it to an assistant.

**For yourself:**

1. Read the first line of the summary. That's the category.
2. Look at the first `•` bullet. That's the main complaint.
3. Look at the source pointer. That's the exact location.
4. Fix it. Rebuild. The wall usually collapses to one small error.

**For your assistant:**

1. Paste the **entire** error — all of it, not just the first line.
2. Say: "Fix the first error in this output. Don't change anything else."
3. Rebuild. If more errors remain, paste the next one.

Do not ask the assistant to "fix all the errors" from a wall of text. It will try to address every message at once and often break things. Fix them one at a time. Each fix usually resolves several downstream errors.

## The feedback loop with AI

Here is the pattern that becomes second nature:

```text
You write a prompt → Assistant generates code → You run cabal build
    ↓                                                    ↓
  (clean)                                          (error)
    ↓                                                    ↓
  Ship it                                     Paste the error back
                                                         ↓
                                              Assistant fixes it
                                                         ↓
                                              You run cabal build again
```

Two things make this loop fast in NeoHaskell:

1. **Errors are specific.** "Non-exhaustive patterns in function update — Patterns of type 'AccountEvent' not matched: MoneyWithdrawn" tells the assistant *exactly* what to do. There is no guessing. Compare this to a Python `TypeError` at runtime with a 50-line stack trace — the assistant has to reason about program state, not just types.

2. **Fixes are small.** Most errors require adding one line (an import), one branch (a pattern match), or one wrapper (`Task.yield`). The assistant does not need to rethink the architecture. It needs to add a missing piece that the compiler identified precisely.

Over time, you'll notice the loop tightening. You'll start preempting errors in your prompts: "make sure to handle every event variant," "don't forget the import for `Array`," "wrap the return value in `Task.yield`." That's not you doing the assistant's job — it's you being a better collaborator because you understand the language's feedback.

## Tooling tips

### Use HLS (the language server)

If HLS is set up in your editor, you see errors inline as you type. This catches most issues before you ever run `cabal build`. The NeoHaskell template ships with HLS config, so it should "just work" when your editor is pointed at the right project.

With an AI assistant, this creates an even tighter loop: you see the error in your editor, tell the assistant about it, and the assistant fixes it without a full rebuild cycle.

### Use `cabal build --ghc-options="-fdefer-type-errors"` for exploration

If you're refactoring and want to keep iterating without fixing every error immediately, you can defer type errors to runtime:

```bash
cabal build --ghc-options="-fdefer-type-errors"
```

This lets broken code compile (and fail at runtime when it hits the deferred error). Use sparingly — it hides problems. But it's useful when you're exploring a large refactor and want to see how far you get before circling back to fix types.

## When an error genuinely confuses you

Rare but real: sometimes an error points to a line that looks obviously correct. The usual causes:

- **A hidden typeclass mismatch.** Some function expects a typeclass you forgot to derive.
- **A type family that doesn't match.** `type instance EntityOf Foo = Bar` but you wrote `Baz` somewhere else.
- **An implicit import conflict.** A function from a different module shadows the one you meant.

When this happens:

1. **Try asking your assistant** with the full error and 10 lines of context. Assistants are good at these — they can see the type family chain that you might miss.
2. **Add an explicit type annotation** to the problematic expression. Often the annotation either fixes the error or produces a better one that reveals the real issue.
3. **Check your `type instance` declarations.** These are the most common source of "the error makes no sense" situations — a typo in a type family instance can produce an error that points somewhere else entirely.

If none of that works, post the error in the [NeoHaskell Discord](https://discord.gg/wDj3UYzec8) with the error message, the relevant code, and what you were trying to do. Someone who has seen the error before will point you at the fix.

## The bigger picture

Error messages are not obstacles. They are **the compiler collaborating with you.** Every error is the language saying "I know what you meant, and here's what doesn't line up yet." In NeoHaskell, the errors are more specific than in most languages because the type system encodes more information — which means the errors carry more actionable detail.

When you work with an AI assistant, the compiler becomes a three-way conversation: you describe intent, the assistant proposes code, the compiler says whether the proposal satisfies the contract. The faster you can read the compiler's part of the conversation, the faster the whole loop runs.

You do not need to memorize every error on this page. You need to know three things:

1. Read the summary first.
2. The fix is almost always one line.
3. If you don't understand the error, paste the whole thing to your assistant — the error is structured enough that the assistant will.

## Where to go from here

- **[Common errors](/guides/common-errors/)** — a catalog organized by what you were doing when the error appeared.
- **[Error handling](/guides/error-handling/)** — runtime errors (a different concern from compile-time errors).
- **[Using AI with NeoHaskell](/getting-started/using-ai/)** — the full AI workflow, including the system prompt that prevents most errors in the first place.
