# event-store.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/event-store.mdx

title: "Event store"
description: "Reference for the event-store backends — InMemory for development, PostgresEventStore for production — plus the EventStore interface."
sidebar:
  order: 8

The event store is where events live. NeoHaskell ships with two backends and a pluggable interface for building your own.

## `InMemory`

The in-memory event store. Fast, zero-config, non-persistent. Ideal for development and tests.

```haskell
import Service.EventStore.InMemory qualified as InMemory

app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withEventStore @() (\_ -> InMemory.new)
    |> ...
```

`InMemory.new` returns a `Task` that constructs a new store. It takes no configuration.

**When to use:**

- Development.
- Unit tests.
- Integration tests.
- Demos.

**When NOT to use:**

- Production. Everything vanishes on restart.

## `PostgresEventStore`

The PostgreSQL-backed event store. Production-ready, ACID-compliant, handles high throughput.

```haskell
import Service.EventStore.Postgres (PostgresEventStore (..))

app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withConfig @MyConfig
    |> Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig
    |> ...

makePostgresConfig :: MyConfig -> PostgresEventStore
makePostgresConfig config =
  PostgresEventStore
    { user = config.dbUser
    , password = config.dbPassword
    , host = config.dbHost
    , databaseName = config.dbName
    , port = config.dbPort
    }
```

### Configuration fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | `Text` | PostgreSQL username. |
| `password` | `Text` | PostgreSQL password. |
| `host` | `Text` | PostgreSQL host. |
| `databaseName` | `Text` | PostgreSQL database name. |
| `port` | `Int` | PostgreSQL port (typically 5432). |

The store manages its own schema — on startup, it verifies the expected tables exist and creates them if not. You don't need to run migrations manually.

### What it creates

The Postgres event store creates a small set of tables:

- `events` — the append-only log of events.
- `streams` — per-stream metadata (position, version).
- `snapshots` — entity snapshots for fast reconstruction.
- Supporting indices and functions.

You don't need to interact with these directly. Treat the event store as an opaque interface.

### Operational notes

- Writes are O(1) per append with a bounded number of index updates.
- Reads are served from the PostgreSQL query planner's cache in practice.
- Snapshots are taken automatically to keep entity reconstruction fast.
- Multi-tenant commands are scoped to per-tenant streams at the store level.

See the [PostgreSQL event store guide](/guides/postgresql-event-store/) for production concerns like sizing, backups, replication, and monitoring.

## The `EventStore` interface

If you want to implement a custom event store, you implement the `EventStore` class in `Service.EventStore.Core`. The interface is:

```haskell
data EventStore event = EventStore
  { insert :: StreamId -> InsertionType -> Array event -> Task Text (Array StreamPosition)
  , readStream :: StreamId -> Task Text (Array (StreamPosition, event))
  , subscribeToAllEvents :: (event -> Task Text Unit) -> Task Text Unit
  -- ... more methods
  }
```

The important operations:

- **`insert`** — append events to a stream, honoring the insertion type (creation, existing, after position, any).
- **`readStream`** — read all events for a specific stream (used for entity reconstruction).
- **`subscribeToAllEvents`** — subscribe to new events as they arrive (used by query subscribers and outbound integrations).

Custom event stores are rare — most users stick with `InMemory` for tests and `PostgresEventStore` for production. But the interface is there if you need to plug into a different backend.

## Switching between stores

Because the interface is the same, switching from in-memory to Postgres is a one-line change:

```haskell
-- Development
|> Application.withEventStore @() (\_ -> InMemory.new)

-- Production
|> Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig
```

Your domain code does not change. Your tests keep running against the in-memory store; your production deployment uses Postgres.

## Test helpers

For integration tests that want to exercise the real event-store interface, use `InMemory.new` directly:

```haskell
it "appends events and reads them back" \_ -> do
  store <- InMemory.new |> Task.mapError toText
  let typedStore = EventStore.castEventStore @MyEvent store
  _ <- typedStore.insert streamId StreamCreation events
  result <- typedStore.readStream streamId
  Array.length result |> shouldBe (Array.length events)
```

## Where to go from here

- **[PostgreSQL event store guide](/guides/postgresql-event-store/)** — production operation.
- **[Tutorial Part 6](/tutorial/06-audit-everything/)** — the moment you switch from in-memory to Postgres.
- **[Services and applications](/reference/services-and-applications/)** — how `withEventStore` fits into the builder.

# for-llms.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/for-llms.mdx

title: "For LLMs"
description: "A dense, machine-readable reference for AI assistants working with NeoHaskell code. Paste relevant sections into your system prompt or context."

This page is a concentrated reference designed for LLM context windows. It repeats the essential information from the rest of the documentation in a dense form, so an AI assistant can load it once and write correct NeoHaskell code without wading through tutorials.

If you are an LLM reading this: follow these rules exactly. If you are a human using an LLM, paste this page (or the relevant section) into your system prompt.

## NeoHaskell in one paragraph

NeoHaskell is a strongly-typed, purely functional language where event sourcing, CQRS, commands, events, entities, queries, services, and integrations are language-level primitives. Commands produce events via a pure `decide` function. State is derived from events via a pure `update` function. Read models (queries) are maintained via `combine` functions. Services wrap commands that share an entity/event type. Applications compose services, queries, transports, and integrations via a builder pattern.

## Style rules (strict)

- Use `|>` for function application, never `$`.
- Use `do` blocks for `Task` computations. `<-` is bind, `Task.yield` is return, `Task.throw` is throw.
- Pattern match with `case ... of`. Never pattern-match in function heads.
- Use `let` inside `do` blocks. Never use `let ... in` or `where` clauses.
- Use `[fmt|Hello #{name}|]` for string interpolation. Never use `++` for strings.
- Commas go at the START of each line in records and lists.
- Imports: `import Core` unqualified (for primitives); everything else qualified (`import Text qualified`).
- Type variable names: descriptive (`forall input output.`), not single letters.

## Type mappings

- `Task err val` instead of `IO a`.
- `Result err ok` instead of `Either a b`.
- `Text` instead of `String`.
- `Array a` instead of `[a]` (user-facing).
- `Map k v` from `Map`, not `Data.Map`.
- `Maybe a` is standard.

## Return values

- `Task.yield value` — return inside `Task`.
- `Task.throw error` — fail inside `Task`.
- `Ok value` / `Err reason` — for `Result`.
- `Decider.acceptNew [events]` / `Decider.acceptExisting [events]` / `Decider.reject "reason"` — for command decisions.

## File layout conventions

```text
src/MyApp/Feature/
├── Core.hs              -- entity and events
├── Commands/
│   └── DoThing.hs       -- one command per file
├── Queries/
│   └── FeatureView.hs   -- one query per file
├── Integrations/
│   └── SomeReactor.hs   -- one integration per file
└── Service.hs           -- assembles commands into a Service
```

## Canonical entity file

```haskell
module MyApp.Feature.Core (
  Feature (..),
  FeatureEvent (..),
  initialState,
) where

import Core
import Json qualified
import Service.Command.Core (Event (..))

data Feature = Feature
  { featureId :: Uuid
  , ...
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show, Eq)

instance Json.FromJSON Feature
instance Json.ToJSON Feature

initialState :: Feature
initialState = Feature { featureId = Uuid.nil, ... }

type instance NameOf Feature = "Feature"

instance Entity Feature where
  initialStateImpl = initialState
  updateImpl = update

data FeatureEvent
  = FeatureCreated { entityId :: Uuid, ... }
  | SomeEvent { entityId :: Uuid, ... }
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)

instance Json.FromJSON FeatureEvent
instance Json.ToJSON FeatureEvent

type instance EventOf Feature = FeatureEvent
type instance EntityOf FeatureEvent = Feature

instance Event FeatureEvent where
  getEventEntityIdImpl event = case event of
    FeatureCreated { entityId } -> entityId
    SomeEvent { entityId } -> entityId

update :: FeatureEvent -> Feature -> Feature
update event feature = case event of
  FeatureCreated { entityId, ... } -> Feature { featureId = entityId, ... }
  SomeEvent { ... } -> feature { ... }
```

## Canonical command file

```haskell
module MyApp.Feature.Commands.DoThing (
  DoThing (..),
  getEntityId,
  decide,
) where

import Core
import Decider qualified
import Json qualified
import Service.Auth (RequestContext)
import Service.Command.Core (TransportsOf)
import Service.CommandExecutor.TH (command)
import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)
import MyApp.Feature.Core

data DoThing = DoThing
  { featureId :: Uuid
  , ...
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show)

instance Json.FromJSON DoThing
instance Json.ToJSON DoThing

getEntityId :: DoThing -> Maybe Uuid
getEntityId cmd = Just cmd.featureId

decide :: DoThing -> Maybe Feature -> RequestContext -> Decision FeatureEvent
decide cmd feature _ctx = case feature of
  Nothing ->
    Decider.reject "Feature does not exist"
  Just f ->
    if -- ... validation ...
      then Decider.reject "reason"
      else
        Decider.acceptExisting
          [ SomeEvent { entityId = cmd.featureId, ... } ]

type instance EntityOf DoThing = Feature
type instance TransportsOf DoThing = '[WebTransport]

command ''DoThing
```

The line `command ''DoThing` at the bottom is mandatory — it generates the wiring. Don't omit it.

## Canonical query file

```haskell
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}

module MyApp.Feature.Queries.FeatureView (
  FeatureView (..),
  canAccess,
  canView,
) where

import Core
import Json qualified
import Service.Query.Auth (QueryAuthError, UserClaims, publicAccess, publicView)
import Service.Query.TH (deriveQuery)
import MyApp.Feature.Core (Feature (..))

data FeatureView = FeatureView
  { featureId :: Uuid
  , ...
  }
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)

instance Json.FromJSON FeatureView
instance Json.ToJSON FeatureView
instance ToSchema FeatureView

canAccess :: Maybe UserClaims -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canAccess = publicAccess

canView :: Maybe UserClaims -> FeatureView -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canView = publicView

deriveQuery ''FeatureView [''Feature]

instance QueryOf Feature FeatureView where
  queryId feature = feature.featureId
  combine feature _existing =
    Update FeatureView
      { featureId = feature.featureId
      , ...
      }
```

## Canonical service file

```haskell
module MyApp.Feature.Service (service) where

import Core
import MyApp.Feature.Commands.DoThing (DoThing)
import MyApp.Feature.Commands.OtherThing (OtherThing)
import MyApp.Feature.Core ()
import Service qualified

service :: Service _ _
service =
  Service.new
    |> Service.command @DoThing
    |> Service.command @OtherThing
```

## Canonical application file

```haskell
module App (app) where

import Core
import MyApp.Config (MyConfig (..))
import MyApp.Feature.Service qualified as Feature
import MyApp.Feature.Queries.FeatureView (FeatureView)
import Service.Application (Application)
import Service.Application qualified as Application
import Service.EventStore.Postgres (PostgresEventStore (..))
import Service.Transport.Web qualified as WebTransport

app :: Application
app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withConfig @MyConfig
    |> Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig
    |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
    |> Application.withService Feature.service
    |> Application.withQuery @FeatureView

makePostgresConfig :: MyConfig -> PostgresEventStore
makePostgresConfig config =
  PostgresEventStore
    { user = config.dbUser
    , password = config.dbPassword
    , host = config.dbHost
    , databaseName = config.dbName
    , port = config.dbPort
    }
```

## Canonical config file

```haskell
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}

module MyApp.Config (MyConfig (..), HasMyConfig) where

import Config (defineConfig)
import Config qualified
import Core

defineConfig
  "MyConfig"
  [ Config.field @Text "dbHost"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL host"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("localhost" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_HOST"
  , Config.field @Int "dbPort"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL port"
      |> Config.defaultsTo (5432 :: Int)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_PORT"
  , Config.field @Text "dbUser"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL user"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("app" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_USER"
  , Config.field @Text "dbPassword"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL password"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("app" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_PASSWORD"
      |> Config.secret
  , Config.field @Text "dbName"
      |> Config.doc "PostgreSQL database"
      |> Config.defaultsTo ("app" :: Text)
      |> Config.envVar "DB_NAME"
  ]
```

## Test file

```haskell
module MyApp.Feature.Commands.DoThingSpec where

import Array qualified
import Core
import Decider (runDecision, DecisionContext (..), CommandResult (..))
import MyApp.Feature.Commands.DoThing (DoThing (..), decide)
import MyApp.Feature.Core
import Service.Auth (RequestContext (..))
import Service.Event (InsertionType (..))
import Task qualified
import Test
import Uuid qualified

runDecide :: DoThing -> Maybe Feature -> Task Text (CommandResult FeatureEvent)
runDecide cmd entity = do
  let ctx = DecisionContext { genUuid = Task.yield Uuid.nil }
  let reqCtx = RequestContext { user = Nothing }
  runDecision ctx (decide cmd entity reqCtx)

spec :: Spec Unit
spec = describe "DoThing" do
  it "rejects when feature does not exist" \_ -> do
    let cmd = DoThing { featureId = Uuid.nil, ... }
    result <- runDecide cmd Nothing
    result |> shouldBe (RejectCommand "Feature does not exist")

  it "accepts and emits expected events" \_ -> do
    let feature = Just (initialState { featureId = Uuid.nil })
    let cmd = DoThing { featureId = Uuid.nil, ... }
    result <- runDecide cmd feature
    case result of
      AcceptCommand _ events ->
        Array.length events |> shouldBe 1
      _ -> Test.fail "Expected AcceptCommand"
```

## Anti-patterns (never do)

- `IO a` — use `Task err val`.
- `Either a b` — use `Result err ok`.
- `pure` / `return` — use `Task.yield`.
- `let ... in` — use `let` inside `do`.
- `where` clauses — use top-level helpers.
- Pattern matching in function heads — use `case`.
- `++` for strings — use `[fmt|...|]`.
- Point-free style — write explicit parameters.
- `$` — use `|>`.
- Custom operators — don't.
- `StateT`, `ReaderT`, other transformers — use `Task` and record passing.
- Code-generation macros except `command ''Foo`, `deriveQuery`, `defineConfig`, `[fmt|...|]`.
- Mixing `InternalTransport` with public transports in the same command.
- Using two different event types in the same service.
- Omitting `entityId` from event constructors.
- Omitting the final `command ''Foo` line in a command file.

## The compile-time guarantees

If your code type-checks, the following are guaranteed:

- `update` handles every event variant.
- `getEventEntityIdImpl` handles every event variant.
- Every command in a service shares the same entity/event type.
- Every registered command's transport is registered with the application.
- Every query's entity list has a corresponding `QueryOf` instance.

If it doesn't type-check, fix the type error and re-verify. The compiler is telling you something real.

# integrations.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/integrations.mdx

title: "Integrations"
description: "Reference for outbound integrations, inbound integrations, timers, and the ToAction typeclass."
sidebar:
  order: 6

## Outbound integrations

Outbound integrations react to domain events and produce actions.

### `OutboundIntegration`

```haskell
class OutboundIntegration integration where
  reactTo ::
    integration ->
    EntityOf integration ->
    EventOf (EntityOf integration) ->
    Integration.Outbound
```

Define one instance per integration type. The `reactTo` function is pure — it takes the config (of type `integration`), the current entity state, and the event that just happened, and returns an `Outbound` collection of actions.

```haskell
data MyIntegration = MyIntegration

type instance EntityOf MyIntegration = User

instance OutboundIntegration MyIntegration where
  reactTo _config user event = case event of
    UserRegistered { email } ->
      Integration.batch
        [ Integration.outbound Sendgrid.Email { to = email, ... } ]
    _ -> Integration.none
```

Register with the application:

```haskell
Application.new
  |> ...
  |> Application.withOutbound @MyIntegration
```

### Outbound construction helpers

```haskell
import Integration qualified
```

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Integration.batch [action1, action2, ...]` | Combine multiple actions into one outbound result. |
| `Integration.none` | No actions for this event. |
| `Integration.outbound config` | Wrap a config record in an action (requires a `ToAction` instance). |
| `Integration.emitCommand cmd` | Action that dispatches a command back into the system. |
| `Integration.noCommand` | Action that produces no follow-up command. |

### The `ToAction` typeclass

```haskell
class ToAction config where
  toAction :: config -> Action
```

Integration package authors (like `Sendgrid`, `Slack`, `Stripe`) implement this. Users just build config records and pass them to `Integration.outbound`.

```haskell
-- Library author (Nick)
instance ToAction Sendgrid.Email where
  toAction config = Integration.action \ctx -> do
    response <- Http.post "https://api.sendgrid.com/..." |> Http.send
    Integration.noCommand

-- Library user (Jess)
Integration.outbound Sendgrid.Email
  { to = "alice@example.com"
  , templateId = "welcome"
  }
```

## Outbound with lifecycle

For integrations that need state across events (rate limiters, batch buffers, token caches), use `withOutboundLifecycle`:

```haskell
Application.new
  |> ...
  |> Application.withOutboundLifecycle @Config @Entity (\config -> runner)
```

See the NeoHaskell testbed for a full example (`EventCounter` integration).

## Inbound integrations

Inbound integrations feed external input into NeoHaskell as commands.

### `Integration.Inbound`

```haskell
newtype Inbound = Inbound InboundInternal
```

You construct one from an `InboundConfig`:

```haskell
data InboundConfig command = InboundConfig
  { run :: (command -> Task IntegrationError Unit) -> Task IntegrationError Unit
  }

myInbound :: Integration.Inbound
myInbound = Integration.inbound
  InboundConfig
    { run = \emit -> do
        -- Do any setup you need
        forever do
          external <- receiveFromQueue
          emit (toCommand external)
    }
```

`run` receives an `emit` callback that dispatches a command into NeoHaskell. Call it whenever you have a command to fire.

Register with the application:

```haskell
Application.withInbound @() (\_ -> myInbound)
```

### Timers

For periodic commands, use the timer helper:

```haskell
import Integration.Timer qualified as Timer
```

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Timer.every config` | Fire a command on a fixed interval. |
| `Timer.seconds n` | A duration of n seconds. |
| `Timer.minutes n` | A duration of n minutes. |
| `Timer.hours n` | A duration of n hours. |

```haskell
dailyReport :: Integration.Inbound
dailyReport =
  Timer.every
    Timer.Every
      { interval = Timer.hours 24
      , toCommand = \_ -> GenerateDailyReport
      }
```

The command is fired through the same executor as external commands — it goes through `decide`, produces events, updates projections, etc.

## Integration errors

```haskell
data IntegrationError
  = NetworkError Text
  | AuthenticationError Text
  | ValidationError Text
  | RateLimited Int       -- retry after N seconds
  | PermanentFailure Text
  | UnexpectedError Text
```

When an integration action fails, it returns one of these. Transient errors (`NetworkError`, `RateLimited`) trigger automatic retries with backoff. Permanent errors (`PermanentFailure`, `ValidationError`) do not — they bubble up for you to handle.

## The `ActionContext`

When an action runs, it receives an `ActionContext`:

```haskell
data ActionContext = ActionContext
  { secretStore :: SecretStore
  , providerRegistry :: ImmutableProviderRegistry
  , refreshLocks :: ConcurrentMap Text Lock
  , fileAccess :: Maybe FileAccessContext
  }
```

This is how actions access:

- Secrets (API keys, tokens) via `SecretStore`.
- OAuth2 provider configs via `providerRegistry`.
- Shared locks for things like OAuth token refresh.
- Uploaded files (if file uploads are enabled).

Most integrations don't need any of this — they just construct an HTTP request and send it. It's available when you do.

## Command payload construction

When an integration emits a command, it packages it as a `CommandPayload`:

```haskell
data CommandPayload = CommandPayload
  { commandType :: Text
  , commandData :: Json.Value
  }
```

You don't usually construct these directly — `Integration.emitCommand` and `Integration.encodeCommand` do it for you.

## Testing integrations

Integrations are pure functions of events to actions, so they test directly:

```haskell
it "emits a welcome email on registration" \_ -> do
  let user = User { ..., email = "alice@example.com" }
  let event = UserRegistered { entityId = aliceId, email = "alice@example.com" }
  let outbound = reactTo WelcomeEmail user event
  Array.length (Integration.getActions outbound) |> shouldBe 1
```

Helpers:

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Integration.getActions outbound` | Extract the list of actions from an `Outbound`. |
| `Integration.runAction ctx action` | Execute an action in a test context. |

## Where to go from here

- **[Integrating existing systems guide](/guides/integrating-existing-systems/)** — practical patterns.
- **[Services and applications](/reference/services-and-applications/)** — how integrations are wired in.
- **[Tutorial Part 5](/tutorial/05-transfers/)** — a full worked example of the saga pattern.

# queries.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/queries.mdx

title: "Queries"
description: "Reference for Query, QueryOf, deriveQuery, combine, and the query auth helpers."
sidebar:
  order: 4

## The `Query` typeclass

```haskell
class Query query where
  canAccessImpl :: Maybe UserClaims -> Maybe QueryAuthError
  canViewImpl :: Maybe UserClaims -> query -> Maybe QueryAuthError
  maxResultsImpl :: Int
  maxResultsImpl = absoluteMaxLimit  -- default: 1000
```

- **`canAccessImpl`** — checked before fetching data. "Can this user access this query type?"
- **`canViewImpl`** — checked after fetching data. "Can this user view this specific instance?"
- **`maxResultsImpl`** — maximum page size for this query type.

You typically don't write this instance by hand. The `deriveQuery` helper generates it from top-level `canAccess` and `canView` functions in your query module.

## The `QueryOf` typeclass

```haskell
class (Entity entity, Query query) => QueryOf entity query where
  queryId :: entity -> Uuid
  combine :: entity -> Maybe query -> QueryAction query
```

One instance per (entity, query) pair. Implements:

- **`queryId`** — what's the key of the query instance this entity contributes to?
- **`combine`** — given the current entity state and the existing query (if any), what's the new query state?

## `QueryAction`

```haskell
data QueryAction query
  = Update query  -- store or replace
  | Delete        -- remove
  | NoOp          -- unchanged
```

What `combine` returns. Three possibilities:

- **`Update newQuery`** — store this as the new value.
- **`Delete`** — remove the query instance.
- **`NoOp`** — take no action.

## The `deriveQuery` helper

```haskell
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}

import Service.Query.TH (deriveQuery)

deriveQuery ''MyQuery [''Entity1, ''Entity2]
```

`deriveQuery` generates:

- The `Query` instance (wiring `canAccess` and `canView` from your top-level functions to the typeclass methods).
- The `NameOf` type instance (derived from the type name, converted to kebab-case).
- The `EntitiesOf` type instance (telling the query subscriber which entities to listen to).
- The `KnownHash` instance for the query name.

You still write the `QueryOf` instances yourself — one for each entity in the list.

## Query auth helpers

```haskell
import Service.Query.Auth
```

| Function | Use case |
|---|---|
| `publicAccess` | Anyone can access (no auth required). |
| `publicView` | Anyone can view any instance. |
| `authenticatedAccess` | Any logged-in user can access. |
| `adminOnlyAccess` | Requires admin claim. |
| `ownerOnly (.ownerField)` | Only the owner (matched via a field accessor) can view. |

These are functions you plug into `canAccess` and `canView`:

```haskell
canAccess :: Maybe UserClaims -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canAccess = authenticatedAccess

canView :: Maybe UserClaims -> MyQuery -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canView = ownerOnly (.ownerId)
```

Return `Nothing` to allow, `Just error` to deny. The helpers handle common cases; for custom logic, write your own function with the same signature.

## Type family

```haskell
type family EntitiesOf (query :: Type) :: [Type]
```

Declares the list of entity types a query depends on. Generated by `deriveQuery` from its second argument.

## A complete example

```haskell
{-# LANGUAGE TemplateHaskell #-}

module MyApp.User.Queries.UserDashboard (
  UserDashboard (..),
  canAccess,
  canView,
) where

import Array qualified
import Core
import Json qualified
import Maybe qualified
import Service.Query.Auth (QueryAuthError, UserClaims, authenticatedAccess, ownerOnly)
import Service.Query.TH (deriveQuery)
import MyApp.User.Core (User (..))
import MyApp.Post.Core (Post (..))

data UserDashboard = UserDashboard
  { userId :: Uuid
  , userName :: Text
  , email :: Text
  , postCount :: Int
  , mostRecentPostTitle :: Maybe Text
  }
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)

instance Json.FromJSON UserDashboard
instance Json.ToJSON UserDashboard
instance ToSchema UserDashboard

canAccess :: Maybe UserClaims -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canAccess = authenticatedAccess

canView :: Maybe UserClaims -> UserDashboard -> Maybe QueryAuthError
canView = ownerOnly (.userId |> Uuid.toText)

deriveQuery ''UserDashboard [''User, ''Post]

instance QueryOf User UserDashboard where
  queryId user = user.userId

  combine user existing =
    Update UserDashboard
      { userId = user.userId
      , userName = user.name
      , email = user.email
      , postCount = existing |> Maybe.map (.postCount) |> Maybe.withDefault 0
      , mostRecentPostTitle =
          existing |> Maybe.andThen (.mostRecentPostTitle)
      }

instance QueryOf Post UserDashboard where
  queryId post = post.authorId

  combine post existing = case existing of
    Nothing ->
      -- User dashboard hasn't been created yet; skip this event.
      NoOp
    Just dashboard ->
      Update dashboard
        { postCount = dashboard.postCount + 1
        , mostRecentPostTitle = Just post.title
        }
```

## HTTP endpoints

Registering a query with `Application.withQuery @MyQuery` generates an HTTP endpoint at:

```text
GET /queries/{query-name}/{id}
```

Where `{query-name}` is the kebab-case form of the query type name (e.g., `UserDashboard` → `user-dashboard`) and `{id}` is the query instance ID (what `queryId` returns).

Pagination is supported via query parameters:

```text
GET /queries/user-dashboard?limit=20&offset=40
```

## Registering queries with the application

```haskell
app :: Application
app =
  Application.new
    |> ...
    |> Application.withQuery @UserDashboard
```

`withQuery` does three things:

1. Registers the query definition with the query registry.
2. Creates the query object store (in-memory by default; use `withQueryObjectStore` to override).
3. Adds an HTTP endpoint.

## Rebuilding queries

On application startup, all queries are rebuilt from the complete event history. If you change a query's shape or logic, the old read models are discarded and replaced with fresh ones. This happens automatically.

For large event stores this rebuild can take a noticeable amount of time. In production, you typically snapshot query state and only rebuild when detecting a version change. See the [PostgreSQL event store guide](/guides/postgresql-event-store/) for details.

## Where to go from here

- **[Queries concept (Updates)](/concepts/updates/)** — the "why" behind queries.
- **[Entities and events](/reference/entities/)** — the write side.
- **[Services and applications](/reference/services-and-applications/)** — how queries are wired in.

# services-and-applications.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/services-and-applications.mdx

title: "Services and applications"
description: "Reference for Service.new, Service.command, Application.new, and every Application.with* builder."
sidebar:
  order: 5

## `Service`

A `Service` bundles commands that share an entity and event type.

```haskell
import Service qualified
```

| Function | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Service.new` | `Service '[] '[]` | Empty service. |
| `Service.command @Cmd` | `Service cmds transports -> Service ... ...` | Register a command type. |

Typical use:

```haskell
service :: Service _ _
service =
  Service.new
    |> Service.command @CreateCart
    |> Service.command @AddItem
    |> Service.command @RemoveItem
    |> Service.command @Checkout
```

The underscores in the return type let the compiler infer the exact type. You can write the full type if you prefer, but it includes type-level lists that are tedious to spell out.

**Compile-time constraint:** all commands must share the same `EntityOf` and `EventOf`. Mixing types produces a custom error message.

## `Application`

An `Application` combines services, queries, integrations, transports, and event-store configuration into a single runnable unit.

```haskell
import Service.Application qualified as Application
import Service.Application (Application)
```

### Construction

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.new` | Empty application. |
| `Application.withConfig @Config` | Register a typed configuration. Must come before factories that depend on it. |

### Event store

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withEventStore @() factory` | Static event-store factory (takes unit config). |
| `Application.withEventStore factory` | Config-dependent factory (takes your app config type). |

### Transports

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withTransport WebTransport.server` | Register the HTTP transport. |
| `Application.withTransport Cli.cli` | Register the CLI transport. |
| `Application.withTransport Mcp.server` | Register the MCP transport. |

Multiple transports can be registered — each runs independently.

### Services

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withService service` | Register a service with all its commands. |
| `Application.withServiceRunner runner` | Register a pre-built `ServiceRunner` (lower-level). |

### Queries

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withQuery @QueryType` | Register a query type for automatic wiring. |
| `Application.withQueryObjectStore config` | Configure the query storage backend. Defaults to in-memory. |
| `Application.withQueryEndpoint name handler` | Register a custom query endpoint (lower-level). |

### Integrations

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withOutbound @Integration` | Register a typed outbound integration. |
| `Application.withOutboundLifecycle @config @Entity factory` | Register a stateful outbound integration with lifecycle. |
| `Application.withInbound @config factory` | Register an inbound integration. |

### Auth and OAuth

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withAuth @config factory` | Enable JWT authentication via an auth server URL. |
| `Application.withAuthOverrides overrides` | Advanced auth customization. |
| `Application.withOAuth2StateKey envVarName` | Set the environment variable holding the OAuth2 HMAC key. |
| `Application.withOAuth2Provider @config factory` | Register an OAuth2 provider. |

### File uploads

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withFileUpload factory` | Enable file upload support with the given config. |

### CORS and API info

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withCors @config factory` | Configure CORS headers. |
| `Application.withApiInfo @config factory` | Set API metadata for the OpenAPI spec. |

### Health check

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withHealthCheck @config factory` | Customize the health check endpoint. |
| `Application.withoutHealthCheck` | Disable the default `/health` endpoint. |

### Secret store

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withSecretStore @config factory` | Configure a secret store for token/credential management. |

### Dispatcher

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.withDispatcherConfig @config factory` | Tune the command dispatcher (worker count, timeouts, etc.). |

### Running

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.run app` | Run the app to completion. Loads config, creates event store, rebuilds queries, starts transports and integrations. |
| `Application.runWith store app` | Run with a pre-built event store (useful for tests). |
| `Application.runWithAsync store app` | Non-blocking run that returns a handle. |

## A complete example

```haskell
module App (app) where

import Core
import MyApp.Config (MyConfig (..))
import MyApp.Integrations.WelcomeEmail (WelcomeEmail)
import MyApp.Queries.UserDashboard (UserDashboard)
import MyApp.Queries.PostFeed (PostFeed)
import MyApp.Services qualified as Services
import Service.Application (Application)
import Service.Application qualified as Application
import Service.EventStore.Postgres (PostgresEventStore (..))
import Service.Transport.Web qualified as WebTransport

app :: Application
app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withConfig @MyConfig
    |> Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig
    |> Application.withAuth getAuthUrl
    |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
    |> Application.withService Services.userService
    |> Application.withService Services.postService
    |> Application.withQuery @UserDashboard
    |> Application.withQuery @PostFeed
    |> Application.withOutbound @WelcomeEmail

getAuthUrl :: MyConfig -> Text
getAuthUrl config = config.authServerUrl

makePostgresConfig :: MyConfig -> PostgresEventStore
makePostgresConfig config =
  PostgresEventStore
    { user = config.dbUser
    , password = config.dbPassword
    , host = config.dbHost
    , databaseName = config.dbName
    , port = config.dbPort
    }
```

`main.hs` then:

```haskell
module Main where

import App (app)
import Core
import Service.Application qualified as Application
import Task qualified

main :: IO ()
main = Task.runMain (Application.run app)
```

## Configuration factory pattern

Many `with*` functions accept either a unit config (`@()`) or a factory that takes your application config type. This lets you defer config-dependent decisions to runtime, after the config has been loaded.

```haskell
-- Static (no config needed)
Application.withEventStore @() (\_ -> InMemory.new)

-- Dynamic (uses MyConfig)
Application.withEventStore makePostgresConfig
```

The second form requires that you also call `withConfig @MyConfig` earlier in the chain. The compiler enforces this.

## Inspection helpers

Useful for debugging and testing the application graph:

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Application.isEmpty app` | `True` if no configuration has been set. |
| `Application.hasEventStore app` | Event store registered? |
| `Application.hasServiceRunners app` | Any services registered? |
| `Application.serviceRunnerCount app` | How many? |
| `Application.hasTransports app` | Any transports registered? |
| `Application.transportCount app` | How many? |
| `Application.hasQueryDefinitions app` | Any queries registered? |
| `Application.queryDefinitionCount app` | How many? |

- **[Integrations](/reference/integrations/)** — reference for the integration builders.
- **[Transports](/reference/transports/)** — what `withTransport` accepts.
- **[Configuration](/reference/configuration/)** — how `withConfig` works.

# testing.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/testing.mdx

title: "Testing"
description: "Reference for the Test module — describe, it, shouldBe, shouldSatisfy, and the test helpers."
sidebar:
  order: 10

NeoHaskell uses Hspec for testing, re-exported via the `Test` module.

```haskell
import Test
```

## Test structure

```haskell
module MyApp.MyFeatureSpec where

import Core
import Test

spec :: Spec Unit
spec = do
  describe "MyFeature" do
    it "does something" \_ -> do
      Task.yield ()

    it "does something else" \_ -> do
      Task.yield ()
```

Every test file exports a `spec :: Spec Unit`. Hspec-discover picks up files named `*Spec.hs` automatically — you don't register them manually.

## Helpers

| Helper | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `describe "label" body` | `Text -> Spec Unit -> Spec Unit` | Group related tests. Nest freely. |
| `it "label" action` | `Text -> (x -> Task Text Unit) -> Spec Unit` | Single test case. |
| `shouldBe expected` | `(Eq a, Show a) => a -> a -> Task Text Unit` | Assert equality. |
| `shouldSatisfy pred` | `(Show a) => (a -> Bool) -> a -> Task Text Unit` | Assert a predicate holds. |
| `Test.fail "message"` | `Text -> Task Text a` | Explicitly fail with a message. |
| `pending "reason"` | `Text -> Task Text Unit` | Mark as pending (not yet implemented). |

Assertions are written as `value |> shouldBe expected`. The pipe reads as "take this value, compare to this expected."

## Writing Given-When-Then tests

The standard pattern for testing a command's `decide` function:

```haskell
import Decider (runDecision, DecisionContext (..), CommandResult (..))
import Service.Auth (RequestContext (..))
import Task qualified
import Uuid qualified

-- Helper: run decide in a test context.
runDecide ::
  MyCommand ->
  Maybe MyEntity ->
  Task Text (CommandResult MyEvent)
runDecide cmd entity = do
  let ctx = DecisionContext { genUuid = Task.yield Uuid.nil }
  let reqCtx = RequestContext { user = Nothing }
  runDecision ctx (decide cmd entity reqCtx)

-- Helper: construct a test entity.
anEntity :: MyEntity
anEntity = MyEntity { ... }

spec :: Spec Unit
spec = describe "MyCommand" do
  it "rejects when entity does not exist" \_ -> do
    let cmd = MyCommand { ... }
    result <- runDecide cmd Nothing
    result |> shouldBe (RejectCommand "Entity does not exist")

  it "accepts valid commands" \_ -> do
    let cmd = MyCommand { ... }
    result <- runDecide cmd (Just anEntity)
    case result of
      AcceptCommand _ events -> do
        Array.length events |> shouldBe 1
      _ -> Test.fail "Expected AcceptCommand"
```

## Testing `update` functions

```haskell
spec :: Spec Unit
spec = describe "Entity.update" do
  it "applies MyEvent correctly" \_ -> do
    let state = initialState { someField = 10 }
    let event = MyEvent { delta = 5 }
    let result = update event state
    result.someField |> shouldBe 15
```

## Testing `combine` functions

```haskell
spec :: Spec Unit
spec = describe "MyQuery.combine" do
  it "projects entity state to query shape" \_ -> do
    let entity = MyEntity { ... }
    case combine entity Nothing of
      Update query -> do
        query.someField |> shouldBe expectedValue
      _ -> Test.fail "Expected Update"
```

## Integration tests with an in-memory event store

For tests that exercise the full command flow (decide + append + project), use `InMemory.new`:

```haskell
import Service.EventStore.InMemory qualified as InMemory

spec :: Spec Unit
spec = describe "End-to-end" do
  it "commands produce the expected projections" \_ -> do
    store <- InMemory.new |> Task.mapError toText
    -- ... dispatch commands through the real executor
    -- ... read back the projection
    -- ... assert
    Task.yield ()
```

## Running tests

```bash
cabal test           # Run all test suites
cabal test nhcore-test-core    # Run a specific suite
```

## Test suite naming

NeoHaskell projects typically have multiple test suites to separate concerns:

| Suite | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `*-test-core` | Pure logic — no external dependencies. Fast. |
| `*-test-service` | Service layer — requires PostgreSQL. Slower. |
| `*-test-integration` | Full integration tests. Slowest. |

Run fast suites on every commit, full suites in CI.

## Where to go from here

- **[Testing guide](/guides/testing/)** — practical recipes.
- **[Testing event-sourced systems (concept)](/concepts/testing-event-sourced-systems/)** — the "why" behind the patterns.
- **[Tutorial Part 2](/tutorial/02-account-rules/)** — your first hands-on test.

# transports.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/reference/transports.mdx

title: "Transports"
description: "Reference for WebTransport, Cli, Mcp, and InternalTransport — how commands are exposed to the outside world."
sidebar:
  order: 7

A **transport** is how commands are delivered from outside the application into the command executor. NeoHaskell ships with several transports; you can also write your own.

## Built-in transports

| Transport | Module | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `WebTransport` | `Service.Transport.Web` | HTTP/JSON REST endpoints. |
| `Cli` | `Service.Transport.Cli` | Command-line subcommands. |
| `Mcp` | `Service.Transport.Mcp` | Model Context Protocol (for AI assistants). |
| `InternalTransport` | `Service.Transport.Internal` | In-process only; not exposed externally. |

## Declaring transports on commands

Each command declares which transports it's available over:

```haskell
type instance TransportsOf MyCommand = '[WebTransport, Cli]
```

The type-level list can contain any number of public transports, or exactly one `InternalTransport`. You cannot mix public and internal transports in the same command — the compiler rejects that with a specific error message.

## `WebTransport`

HTTP/JSON REST. Commands become `POST /commands/CommandName`, and queries become `GET /queries/query-name/:id`.

```haskell
import Service.Transport.Web qualified as WebTransport

app =
  Application.new
    |> ...
    |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
```

`WebTransport.server` is the default configuration. Customize it by passing a configured value:

```haskell
let webTransport = WebTransport.server
      { WebTransport.port = 8080
      , WebTransport.host = "0.0.0.0"
      }
in Application.withTransport webTransport
```

### Features

- **Automatic OpenAPI spec** at `/openapi.json`.
- **Swagger UI** at `/docs` (in development mode).
- **Health check** at `/health` (configurable).
- **OAuth2 callback routes** if `withOAuth2Provider` is registered.
- **CORS** if `withCors` is configured.
- **JWT auth** if `withAuth` is configured.

## `Cli`

Command-line interface. Commands become subcommands of the binary; arguments map to command fields.

```haskell
import Service.Transport.Cli qualified as Cli

app =
  Application.new
    |> ...
    |> Application.withTransport Cli.cli
```

With a `Deposit` command, you'd invoke it as:

```bash
./your-app deposit --account-id "abc-123" --amount 50
```

The Cli transport automatically parses JSON-schema-compatible fields as command-line options.

## `Mcp`

Model Context Protocol. Exposes commands and queries as MCP tools for AI assistants.

```haskell
import Service.Transport.Mcp qualified as Mcp

app =
  Application.new
    |> ...
    |> Application.withTransport Mcp.server
```

The MCP transport uses STDIO by default (suitable for local integration with Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.). Each command becomes an MCP tool that the assistant can call; each query becomes a readable resource.

## `InternalTransport`

Used for commands that should only be invoked from inside the application — typically by integrations, not by external clients.

```haskell
import Service.Transport.Internal (InternalTransport)

type instance TransportsOf RecordWithdrawal = '[InternalTransport]
```

Internal commands:

- Are NOT exposed over HTTP, CLI, or MCP.
- Can still be dispatched via `Integration.emitCommand`.
- Are included in the command dispatch map so integrations can address them.
- Can include exactly one `InternalTransport`, never mixed with public transports.

This is the right choice for commands like `FailTransfer`, `CompleteOrder`, or other state-machine transitions that should not be user-triggered.

## Running multiple transports

You can register as many transports as you want. Commands declare which transports they're available over; the application registers transports at the app level. The intersection determines which commands are actually exposed on which transports.

```haskell
app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
    |> Application.withTransport Cli.cli
    |> Application.withTransport Mcp.server
    |> Application.withService service
```

A command declared as `TransportsOf = '[WebTransport]` is exposed only over HTTP. A command declared as `'[WebTransport, Cli]` is exposed over both. A command declared as `'[InternalTransport]` is exposed over none.

## Writing a custom transport

You can implement the `Transport` typeclass to support additional protocols — gRPC, WebSockets, message queues, etc. This is more advanced and typically reserved for integration library authors rather than application developers. See `Service.Transport.Internal` for the class definition.

## Where to go from here

- **[Services and applications](/reference/services-and-applications/)** — how to register transports with the app.
- **[Commands and decisions](/reference/commands/)** — how to declare transports on commands.
- **[Tutorial Part 6](/tutorial/06-audit-everything/)** — an example of running multiple transports together.

# 01-first-transaction.mdx

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/tutorial/01-first-transaction.mdx

title: "Part 1 — Your first transaction"
description: "Open a bank account, deposit money, derive the balance from events. Your first NeoBank feature in about 60 lines of code."

import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**What you'll build in this part:** A working banking service where you can open an account, deposit money into it, and ask for the balance. All three features — opening, depositing, and balance queries — come from a single event stream. You will not store a balance anywhere. You will derive it.

**Reading time:** ~20 minutes · **Lines of code:** ~60

## What you'll learn

- How to define an **entity** (the thing whose state you care about — here, an `Account`).
- How to define **events** (immutable facts about what happened).
- How to define **commands** (requests to do something).
- How to write a **decide** function (accept or reject a command, producing events).
- How to write an **update** function (fold events into state).
- How to wire everything into a running application.

## The CRUD code that fails

Before we start, think about how you'd write this in a database-first style. You'd have an `accounts` table with an `id` column, an `owner` column, and a `balance` column. A deposit would be:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 'abc-123';
```

Done? Not really. Imagine a year passes and legal asks: "what was the balance of account abc-123 at 3pm last Tuesday?" You can't answer. You threw the history away.

This is the bug NeoHaskell fixes by default. Let's build the correct version.

## Step 1 — The entity and its events

We need to define two things: what an `Account` is, and what events can happen to it. Create the file `src/NeoBank/Account/Core.hs`:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Core (
  Account (..),
  AccountEvent (..),
  initialState,
) where

import Core
import Json qualified
import Service.Command.Core (Event (..))

-- | An account — the thing whose state we care about.
data Account = Account
  { accountId :: Uuid
  , ownerName :: Text
  , balance :: Int
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show, Eq)

instance Json.FromJSON Account
instance Json.ToJSON Account

-- | Every account starts empty.
initialState :: Account
initialState =
  Account
    { accountId = Uuid.nil
    , ownerName = ""
    , balance = 0
    }

type instance NameOf Account = "Account"

instance Entity Account where
  initialStateImpl = initialState
  updateImpl = update

-- | Events — the immutable facts that can happen to an account.
data AccountEvent
  = AccountOpened
      { entityId :: Uuid
      , ownerName :: Text
      }
  | MoneyDeposited
      { entityId :: Uuid
      , amount :: Int
      }
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)

instance Json.FromJSON AccountEvent
instance Json.ToJSON AccountEvent

type instance EventOf Account = AccountEvent
type instance EntityOf AccountEvent = Account

instance Event AccountEvent where
  getEventEntityIdImpl event = case event of
    AccountOpened { entityId } -> entityId
    MoneyDeposited { entityId } -> entityId

-- | The heart of event sourcing: fold an event into the entity state.
update :: AccountEvent -> Account -> Account
update event account = case event of
  AccountOpened { entityId, ownerName } ->
    Account
      { accountId = entityId
      , ownerName = ownerName
      , balance = 0
      }
  MoneyDeposited { amount } ->
    account { balance = account.balance + amount }
```

Read that one more time with the understanding that **this is the whole spec for what an account is**. The field list is the shape of state. The event list is the shape of every change that can happen. The `update` function is how each change takes effect. There is no database schema. There is no migration. There is this file.

<Aside type="note" title="Why do events carry entityId?">
Every event has to know which stream it belongs to. `entityId` is how the event store routes events into the right stream. Without it, the system wouldn't know which account a deposit affected.
</Aside>

## Step 2 — The OpenAccount command

Commands are how the outside world asks the bank to do things. Our first command is `OpenAccount`. Create `src/NeoBank/Account/Commands/OpenAccount.hs`:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Commands.OpenAccount (
  OpenAccount (..),
  getEntityId,
  decide,
) where

import Core
import Decider qualified
import Json qualified
import Service.Auth (RequestContext)
import Service.Command.Core (TransportsOf)
import Service.CommandExecutor.TH (command)
import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)
import NeoBank.Account.Core

-- | The command: "I want to open an account for this person."
data OpenAccount = OpenAccount
  { ownerName :: Text
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show)

instance Json.FromJSON OpenAccount
instance Json.ToJSON OpenAccount

-- | Account creation: we don't know the ID yet (we're creating it).
getEntityId :: OpenAccount -> Maybe Uuid
getEntityId _ = Nothing

-- | The decision: accept the command, producing an AccountOpened event.
decide :: OpenAccount -> Maybe Account -> RequestContext -> Decision AccountEvent
decide cmd existing _ctx = case existing of
  Just _ ->
    Decider.reject "Account already exists"
  Nothing -> do
    newId <- Decider.generateUuid
    Decider.acceptNew
      [ AccountOpened
          { entityId = newId
          , ownerName = cmd.ownerName
          }
      ]

type instance EntityOf OpenAccount = Account
type instance TransportsOf OpenAccount = '[WebTransport]

command ''OpenAccount
```

Walk through what just happened.

- `data OpenAccount = OpenAccount { ownerName :: Text }` — the shape of the request.
- `getEntityId _ = Nothing` — this command is *creating* an account, so there's no existing ID to target.
- `decide` — the business logic. If an account already exists at this ID, we reject. Otherwise we generate a UUID and emit an `AccountOpened` event. **We do not touch any balance field. The event is the only thing that happens.**
- The type-family lines (`type instance EntityOf ...`) tell the compiler which entity this command affects and which transports carry it.
- `command ''OpenAccount` — that last line is a code-generation macro that produces the HTTP endpoint, JSON schema, handler registration, and everything else. You write domain logic; the macro generates the wiring.

<Aside type="tip" title="Why the double-tick?">
`''OpenAccount` (with two ticks) is the syntax for "the name `OpenAccount` as a value the macro can work with." You don't need to understand how it works — just know that every command file ends with this line.
</Aside>

## Step 3 — The Deposit command

Create `src/NeoBank/Account/Commands/Deposit.hs`:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Commands.Deposit (
  Deposit (..),
  getEntityId,
  decide,
) where

import Core
import Decider qualified
import Json qualified
import Service.Auth (RequestContext)
import Service.Command.Core (TransportsOf)
import Service.CommandExecutor.TH (command)
import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)
import NeoBank.Account.Core

-- | The command: "Deposit this much into this account."
data Deposit = Deposit
  { accountId :: Uuid
  , amount :: Int
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show)

instance Json.FromJSON Deposit
instance Json.ToJSON Deposit

-- | This command targets an existing account, so we return its ID.
getEntityId :: Deposit -> Maybe Uuid
getEntityId cmd = Just cmd.accountId

-- | Business rules:
--   - The account must exist.
--   - The amount must be positive.
decide :: Deposit -> Maybe Account -> RequestContext -> Decision AccountEvent
decide cmd account _ctx = case account of
  Nothing ->
    Decider.reject "Account does not exist"
  Just _ ->
    if cmd.amount <= 0
      then Decider.reject "Deposit amount must be positive"
      else
        Decider.acceptExisting
          [ MoneyDeposited
              { entityId = cmd.accountId
              , amount = cmd.amount
              }
          ]

type instance EntityOf Deposit = Account
type instance TransportsOf Deposit = '[WebTransport]

command ''Deposit
```

Notice the difference between `OpenAccount` and `Deposit`:

- `OpenAccount` uses `acceptNew` — "only accept this if the account doesn't exist yet." This is creation.
- `Deposit` uses `acceptExisting` — "only accept this if the account does exist." This is modification.

The event store enforces these guarantees. If two `OpenAccount` commands race each other, only one wins — the other gets a rejection. You get that for free.

## Step 4 — The service

A service bundles related commands together. Create `src/NeoBank/Account/Service.hs`:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Service (service) where

import Core
import NeoBank.Account.Commands.Deposit (Deposit)
import NeoBank.Account.Commands.OpenAccount (OpenAccount)
import NeoBank.Account.Core ()
import Service qualified

service :: Service _ _
service =
  Service.new
    |> Service.command @OpenAccount
    |> Service.command @Deposit
```

Read this as "make a new service, then register `OpenAccount` and `Deposit` commands in it." The `_` underscores in the return type let the compiler infer the exact type — you don't have to spell it out.

<Aside type="note" title="Why can't I list two different entity types in one service?">
Every command in a service must share the same entity and event type. If you mix types, the compiler will tell you so with an error that says exactly which command is wrong. This is a feature — a service is a consistency boundary, and mixing boundaries is a modeling error.
</Aside>

## Step 5 — Wire it into the application

Open `src/App.hs` and replace its contents with:

```haskell
module App (app) where

import Core
import Service.Application (Application)
import Service.Application qualified as Application
import Service.EventStore.InMemory qualified as InMemory
import Service.Transport.Web qualified as WebTransport
import NeoBank.Account.Service qualified as Account

app :: Application
app =
  Application.new
    |> Application.withEventStore @() (\_ -> InMemory.new)
    |> Application.withTransport WebTransport.server
    |> Application.withService Account.service
```

We're using an in-memory event store. It loses everything on restart. In Part 6 we'll switch to PostgreSQL — it's a one-line change.

## Step 6 — Run it

```bash
cabal build
cabal run
```

Your NeoBank is now listening on port 8080. Open a second terminal and open an account:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/commands/OpenAccount \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ownerName": "Alice"}'
```

You should get back something like:

```json
{
  "kind": "Accepted",
  "entityId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567",
  "events": [
    {
      "kind": "AccountOpened",
      "entityId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567",
      "ownerName": "Alice"
    }
  ]
}
```

Copy that `entityId` — you'll need it to deposit money. Run:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/commands/Deposit \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accountId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567", "amount": 50}'
```

You should see:

```json
{
  "kind": "Accepted",
  "entityId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567",
  "events": [
    {
      "kind": "MoneyDeposited",
      "entityId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567",
      "amount": 50
    }
  ]
}
```

Deposit another 25:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/commands/Deposit \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accountId": "3f5a7b2c-1234-4567-89ab-cdef01234567", "amount": 25}'
```

Now — and this is the point of the whole exercise — **there is no `balance` column anywhere in this system.** Not in the database. Not in the event store. Nowhere. The account's current balance is `50 + 25 = 75` because we can fold the event stream. The events are the truth. The balance is computed on demand.

## Check your understanding

Which of these best describes what an event is in NeoHaskell?

1. A log message for debugging.
2. An immutable fact about something that happened in the domain.
3. A notification sent to another service.
4. A database row that gets updated.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the answer</summary>

**The correct answer is #2: an immutable fact about something that happened in the domain.**

Here is why the other answers are wrong:

- **#1 — Log message.** Events aren't log messages. You can't delete them, filter them by severity, or drop them when disk is full. The entire state of your system derives from them.
- **#3 — Notification.** Events might trigger notifications later (through integrations — we'll cover those in Part 5), but the event itself is a recorded fact, not a message.
- **#4 — Database row that gets updated.** Events are append-only. They are *never* updated. That's the whole point — if you could mutate an event, you'd lose the history.

</details>

Hold on to this mental model. It is the single most important thing in event sourcing.

## What you just built

- Two commands — `OpenAccount` and `Deposit`.
- Two events — `AccountOpened` and `MoneyDeposited`.
- One entity — `Account`.
- A working HTTP service that accepts commands and stores events.
- A balance that is *derived* from events, not stored.

All of that is about 60 lines of code.

## The compiler protection you are already getting

Try this: open `Core.hs` and add a new event variant without updating the `update` function:

```haskell
data AccountEvent
  = AccountOpened { entityId :: Uuid, ownerName :: Text }
  | MoneyDeposited { entityId :: Uuid, amount :: Int }
  | MoneyWithdrawn { entityId :: Uuid, amount :: Int }  -- new
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)
```

Save, run `cabal build`, and watch:

```text
error: [GHC-18872]
    Non-exhaustive patterns in function update

    In an equation for 'update':
        Patterns of type 'AccountEvent' not matched:
            MoneyWithdrawn{}
```

The compiler knows `update` doesn't handle the new case. No runtime error, no failing test, no surprise in production. It knows, now, at build time, with the exact line number.

Revert that change before moving on (or add a `MoneyWithdrawn` case that subtracts — we'll formalize this in the next part).

## Recap

- **Events are facts.** We recorded `AccountOpened` and `MoneyDeposited`. They are immutable and append-only.
- **State is derived.** The balance is a fold over events via `update`. There is no balance field in storage.
- **Commands are intents.** `OpenAccount` and `Deposit` are requests; `decide` decides whether to accept them.
- **Pure functions do the work.** `decide` and `update` are both pure — no database access, no I/O, trivial to test.
- **The compiler enforces the contract.** Missing an event handler is a compile error.

## Next

You have an account. You can deposit into it. But our bank is currently a one-way street — you can only put money in. That is a bad bank. In Part 2, we add withdrawals, and we use the type system to make overdrafts impossible.

[**Part 2 — Account rules →**](/tutorial/02-account-rules/)

# Copy the entityId

Source: https://github.com/neohaskell/neohaskell/blob/main/website/src/content/docs/tutorial/02-account-rules.mdx

title: "Part 2 — Account rules"
description: "Add withdrawals and overdraft protection. Let the compiler catch an illegal-state bug. Write your first Given-When-Then tests."

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**What you'll build in this part:** Withdrawals, with a rule that says you cannot go negative. We will let the compiler catch a bug we accidentally-on-purpose introduce. Then we'll write the first tests — Given-When-Then style, zero mocks.

**Reading time:** ~25 minutes · **Lines of code added:** ~50

## What you'll learn

- How to add a new event to an existing entity.
- How to add a new command and let the compiler verify nothing else is broken.
- How to express business rules in `decide` functions.
- How to write Given-When-Then tests for commands.
- The most important naming rule for events.

## The rule

**Customers can withdraw money, but only if they have enough balance. No overdrafts.**

This is a business rule. In a traditional system it would live in several places — maybe a database constraint, maybe a service-layer check, maybe a frontend validation. In NeoHaskell it lives in exactly one place: the `decide` function of the `Withdraw` command. And the compiler will verify the rest of the code is consistent with it.

## Step 1 — Add the event

Open `src/NeoBank/Account/Core.hs` and add a new variant to `AccountEvent`:

```haskell
data AccountEvent
  = AccountOpened
      { entityId :: Uuid
      , ownerName :: Text
      }
  | MoneyDeposited
      { entityId :: Uuid
      , amount :: Int
      }
  | MoneyWithdrawn
      { entityId :: Uuid
      , amount :: Int
      }
  deriving (Eq, Show, Generic)
```

Save. Run `cabal build`. You should see:

```text
error: [GHC-18872]
    Non-exhaustive patterns in function update

    In an equation for 'update':
        Patterns of type 'AccountEvent' not matched:
            MoneyWithdrawn{}
```

Good. That is the compiler protecting you. It knows you added a new event and it knows you haven't taught `update` what to do with it. This is exactly the bug that bites people who use event sourcing as a library in other languages. The library doesn't know your event type changed, so it can't warn you. The compiler does.

Also remember `getEventEntityIdImpl` — it pattern-matches on every event too, so it needs to know about the new variant. Add both:

```haskell
update :: AccountEvent -> Account -> Account
update event account = case event of
  AccountOpened { entityId, ownerName } ->
    Account
      { accountId = entityId
      , ownerName = ownerName
      , balance = 0
      }
  MoneyDeposited { amount } ->
    account { balance = account.balance + amount }
  MoneyWithdrawn { amount } ->
    account { balance = account.balance - amount }

instance Event AccountEvent where
  getEventEntityIdImpl event = case event of
    AccountOpened { entityId } -> entityId
    MoneyDeposited { entityId } -> entityId
    MoneyWithdrawn { entityId } -> entityId
```

Rebuild. Green.

<Aside type="note" title="Why is update safe to compute negative balances?">
`update` is a **state reconstruction** function — it has to be able to replay any sequence of events, even historical ones. If our bank later relaxes the no-overdraft rule, we want old events to still replay correctly. The *rule* against overdrafts lives in `decide`, which is where business logic belongs. The `update` function is just math.
</Aside>

## Step 2 — The Withdraw command

Create `src/NeoBank/Account/Commands/Withdraw.hs`:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Commands.Withdraw (
  Withdraw (..),
  getEntityId,
  decide,
) where

import Core
import Decider qualified
import Json qualified
import Service.Auth (RequestContext)
import Service.Command.Core (TransportsOf)
import Service.CommandExecutor.TH (command)
import Service.Transport.Web (WebTransport)
import NeoBank.Account.Core

-- | The command: "Withdraw this much from this account."
data Withdraw = Withdraw
  { accountId :: Uuid
  , amount :: Int
  }
  deriving (Generic, Show)

instance Json.FromJSON Withdraw
instance Json.ToJSON Withdraw

getEntityId :: Withdraw -> Maybe Uuid
getEntityId cmd = Just cmd.accountId

-- | Business rules:
--   - The account must exist.
--   - The amount must be positive.
--   - The account must have at least that much balance.
decide :: Withdraw -> Maybe Account -> RequestContext -> Decision AccountEvent
decide cmd account _ctx = case account of
  Nothing ->
    Decider.reject "Account does not exist"
  Just acc ->
    if cmd.amount <= 0
      then Decider.reject "Withdrawal amount must be positive"
      else if cmd.amount > acc.balance
        then Decider.reject "Insufficient funds"
        else
          Decider.acceptExisting
            [ MoneyWithdrawn
                { entityId = cmd.accountId
                , amount = cmd.amount
                }
            ]

type instance EntityOf Withdraw = Account
type instance TransportsOf Withdraw = '[WebTransport]

command ''Withdraw
```

The business rules are the three guards inside `decide`. There is nowhere else for the rule to live. No middleware layer. No database trigger. No frontend validator. The compiler checks the types; the three `if` statements check the rules.

## Step 3 — Register it

Open `src/NeoBank/Account/Service.hs` and add the new command:

```haskell
module NeoBank.Account.Service (service) where

import Core
import NeoBank.Account.Commands.Deposit (Deposit)
import NeoBank.Account.Commands.OpenAccount (OpenAccount)
import NeoBank.Account.Commands.Withdraw (Withdraw)
import NeoBank.Account.Core ()
import Service qualified

service :: Service _ _
service =
  Service.new
    |> Service.command @OpenAccount
    |> Service.command @Deposit
    |> Service.command @Withdraw
```

```bash
cabal build

```

Open an account, deposit 100, try to withdraw 150:

